prompt: A regional insurer receives about 2,000 first-notice-of-loss emails a day. For each one the team wants to extract the policy number, loss date and loss type, look the policy up in the claims system, and file a structured claim record. The steps are the same for every email and the business wants per-step audit logs. Which architecture fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow of sequenced model calls, with the policy lookup done in code between steps
An autonomous agent that reads each email, picks the tools it needs and plans its own sequence of actions
An orchestrator model that spawns one specialist agent per field to extract and then merges their outputs
A single prompt holding the email, the full claims schema and the entire policy register, answered in one call

explanation: Correct: A. The task is fully known in advance and never branches, so a fixed workflow (prompt chaining) gives predictable behaviour, a log line per step and a cheap place to validate between steps. B spends tokens and risk on planning a path that is already known. C adds multi-agent coordination for a three-field extraction that one call handles well. D stuffs the whole policy register into context on every email, which is slow, expensive and impossible to audit step by step.

prompt: A law firm wants an assistant that answers partners' questions about ongoing matters. Some questions need one document lookup, others need a dozen searches across filings, a date calculation and a draft memo, and the path is only clear once early results come back. Which pattern should the architect start from?

options.text: A routing workflow that classifies each question and dispatches it to one of four hand-built pipelines
A parallel workflow that runs every search the firm supports at once and has the model merge the results
An agent loop that calls search and calculation tools, observes results and decides the next step
A prompt chain with a fixed sequence of search, calculate and draft steps applied to every question

explanation: Correct: C. When the number and order of steps depend on what earlier steps reveal, an agent that acts, observes tool results and re-plans is the pattern that fits; the stopping condition and tool budget are then the controls to design. A works when the set of paths is small and known, which is not the case here. B wastes calls on searches that most questions do not need. D cannot adapt when a search turns up nothing or something unexpected.

prompt: A bank's customer-messaging assistant receives a mix of balance questions, fraud reports, mortgage enquiries and complaints. Each type needs different tools, a different tone and different escalation rules, and the team wants to tune one type without regressing the others. Which workflow pattern addresses this most directly?

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one model drafts the reply and a second critiques it until it passes the rules
Prompt chaining: each message passes through tone, tools and escalation steps in one fixed order
Parallelisation: all four specialist prompts answer every message and the best reply is chosen by vote
Routing: a first call classifies the message and hands it to a prompt and tool set built for that type

explanation: Correct: D. Routing separates concerns: each downstream prompt stays small and specific, and changing the complaints handler cannot affect the mortgage handler. A improves the quality of one reply but does not separate the four cases. C quadruples cost and lets the wrong specialist's tools run on every message. B forces a single sequence onto messages that need different tools and rules.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company asks Claude to review 300-page clinical study reports against a 70-item regulatory checklist in a single call. Reviewers find that items near the end of the checklist are often skipped and that findings are inconsistent between runs. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores the checklist more thoroughly on each run
Have the model restate all 70 checklist items before it begins so that none of them are forgotten
Move the single-call design to a larger model with a longer context window
Split the review into calls per checklist section over the relevant report parts

explanation: Correct: D. Skipped late items and run-to-run variance are the classic signs of a task that is too large for one pass. Decomposing by checklist section (a sectioning form of parallelisation) gives each call a bounded job, makes the output comparable between runs and lets each section be evaluated on its own. A adds randomness, the opposite of consistency. B spends tokens restating the checklist without reducing the work per call. C may help at the margin but leaves the structural overload in place.

prompt: A travel company's booking agent must coordinate flight search, hotel search, visa checks and payment. Each sub-task needs its own tools and a long domain prompt. The business wants an ordered record of every step, no payment attempted if the visa check fails, and the orchestration logic visible and testable in code rather than left to the model. Which design meets this?

options.text: A single agent with all the tools registered and one system prompt that covers all four domains
Four independent agents that watch a shared message queue and act when they see a relevant task
An orchestrator in application code that calls four specialist sub-agents in sequence with scoped context
A supervisor model given the four sub-agents as tools, deciding at runtime which to call and in what order

explanation: Correct: C. When the business wants orchestration that is inspectable and unit-testable, put the control flow in code and keep the model inside each specialist step: the code records each outcome in order and stops the sequence when a step fails, and each sub-agent sees a narrow context, which also improves tool selection. A reproduces the bloated-context problem that decomposition is meant to solve. B makes the sequence emergent, so neither the ordering nor the halt can be guaranteed. D is a legitimate orchestrator-workers pattern, but it moves the control flow into the model, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.

prompt: A research-synthesis product uses an orchestrator model that breaks a question into sub-questions, spawns a worker per sub-question, and writes the final report. Reports are good but cost has tripled since launch, and traces show workers repeatedly fetching the same sources. Which change best addresses the cost without changing the pattern?

options.text: Give the orchestrator a shared results store and dedupe sub-questions before spawning
Replace the workers with a single model call that answers every sub-question in one pass
Lower each worker's maximum output tokens so that the repeated fetches cost less per worker
Switch the orchestrator to the smallest model so that planning and decomposition cost less per report

explanation: Correct: A. The waste is duplicated work between workers, so the fix is shared state and deduplication at the orchestration layer; the orchestrator-workers shape stays intact. B abandons the pattern and reintroduces the overload that motivated it. C trims output, but the duplicated fetches are input and tool cost, not output. D saves little, because the orchestrator makes few calls, and risks worse decomposition, which produces more duplicated work rather than less.

prompt: A utility company's chief operating officer lists nine possible first AI projects, from an internal policy chatbot to automated outage-cause analysis. What should most strongly determine which project the architect recommends first?

options.text: Which project shows the largest projected cost saving on paper in the business case
Which project the executive sponsor is personally most enthusiastic about championing
Which project has a measurable outcome, available data and a tolerable cost of error
Which project can run fully automated with no human review step in the loop at all

explanation: Correct: C. A first project should be one where value can be measured, the data exists, and a wrong answer is recoverable; that is what lets the organisation learn and build trust. A looks at value but ignores whether the data exists and whether a wrong answer is recoverable. B matters for sponsorship but is not the primary selection criterion. D treats removing humans as the goal, which raises risk on the very first delivery.

prompt: A procurement assistant has been live for a quarter. Dashboards show cost, latency and uptime, but nobody can say whether its supplier recommendations are being accepted or overridden by buyers. Which addition completes the architecture?

options.text: A feedback loop capturing buyer accept/override decisions into the evaluation set and prompt iteration
A second model that re-scores each recommendation independently and flags any disagreements for review
A larger context window so the assistant can see more supplier history on every single request
A weekly export of all prompts and responses to the data team for long-term archiving and reporting

explanation: Correct: A. An end-to-end architecture runs input, processing, output and a feedback loop; without the loop the team cannot learn whether outputs are right in production. B adds a second opinion but still never learns what buyers actually did. C changes inputs without measuring outcomes. D stores data but creates no signal or loop back into the system.

prompt: A manufacturer wants Claude to answer engineers' questions about 40,000 maintenance manuals that are updated by suppliers every month. Which approach gives the model access to this material in a way that stays current?

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the manuals and retrain it each time a supplier sends an updated manual
An augmented LLM that retrieves relevant manual sections at query time from a refreshed index
Summarise all the manuals into one 150,000-token document and place it in every system prompt
Ask engineers to paste the relevant manual pages into the conversation alongside each question they ask

explanation: Correct: B. Retrieval over a refreshed index is the standard way to give a model large, changing knowledge: the model sees only what is relevant and the index, not the model, is what gets updated. A bakes knowledge into weights that go stale monthly and is costly to repeat. C cannot hold 40,000 manuals and loses detail in the summary. D moves the retrieval problem onto the user.

prompt: A single internal agent handles facilities requests, expense queries and software access requests. It has 40 tools and a 7,000-token system prompt, and it has started picking the wrong tool as capabilities were added. What should the architect do?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt listing which of the 40 tools belong to which of the three domains
Split the agent by domain behind a router, each specialist carrying only its own tools and prompt
Increase the maximum number of tool-use turns so the agent can recover after a wrong first tool choice
Rename every tool with a domain prefix such as `hr_` or `it_` and keep the single agent as it is

explanation: Correct: B. Tool-selection accuracy degrades as a tool set grows and overlaps; decomposing by domain shrinks each agent's choice set and prompt, which fixes the cause. A and D are prompt-level patches that leave 40 tools in every call. C makes wrong choices cheaper to recover from but does not make them rarer, and adds latency and cost.

prompt: A marketing team wants an assistant that writes product descriptions meeting a strict style guide. Drafts are usually close but fail a few rules, and a human currently fixes them by hand. The team can describe the rules precisely. Which pattern automates the fix-up most directly?

options.text: Routing: send each request to a different prompt depending on the product category it belongs to
Evaluator-optimizer: a checker tests the draft against the rules and the writer revises until it passes
Parallelisation: generate five drafts simultaneously and show the human reviewer all of them to choose between
Multi-agent: one specialist agent per style rule, each rewriting the draft for its own rule in turn

explanation: Correct: B. When evaluation criteria are clear and iteration demonstrably improves output, the evaluator-optimizer loop is the fit: generate, check against explicit rules, revise, with a bounded retry count. A changes who writes but not how violations get caught. C produces more drafts for the human to fix rather than fewer. D is far more machinery than a rules check needs and makes the rules interact unpredictably.

prompt: A logistics provider's leadership frames an AI programme around five pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance SLAs. The architect proposes an assistant that drafts customs declarations which clerks then check. Under which pillar should the business case primarily be made, and what metric supports it?

options.text: Transformation, measured by the number of new customer-facing services launched in the year
Cost, measured by the number of tokens consumed per customs declaration drafted
Efficiency, measured by clerk minutes per declaration and first-pass acceptance at customs
Performance SLA, measured by the model's p95 response latency on each declaration

explanation: Correct: C. Drafting for a human to check is an efficiency play on an existing process, and the honest metrics are the time saved per unit and whether quality held (acceptance rate). A describes a different kind of initiative that creates new offerings. B measures the solution's own running cost, not business value. D is a technical constraint to meet, not the reason to build it.

prompt: An agent that reconciles invoices against purchase orders occasionally runs for 40 tool calls on a single invoice before giving up, and a few runs have issued duplicate credit notes. The business accepts some manual fallback. Which pair of architectural controls should the architect add?

options.text: A longer system prompt explaining when to stop, plus a note asking the agent to avoid duplicate credit notes
A turn budget with a hand-off to a human queue, and an idempotency key on the credit-note tool
A second supervising agent that watches the first one's actions and intervenes when it misbehaves
Removing every tool that writes to the finance system and returning to a drafting-only assistant

explanation: Correct: B. Agents need engineered stopping conditions and safe tools: a turn budget with an explicit fallback bounds cost, and idempotent write tools make a retried or repeated action harmless. A relies on instructions to enforce what should be enforced by code. C adds a second non-deterministic component to police the first. D over-corrects; the business accepted automation with fallback, not the removal of it.

prompt: A support team wants each inbound customer email summarised into a three-line CRM note. The CRM already fetches the customer's account record and supplies it with the email, and nothing else is needed. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A prompt chain that extracts entities, then classifies the email, then writes the note in three sequenced calls
An agent loop with CRM search tools, so the model can look up whatever account history it decides it needs
An orchestrator that hands the email to a specialist sub-agent per product line and merges their notes
A single augmented call: one prompt holding the email and the supplied account record, returning the note

explanation: Correct: D. One transformation whose context is already supplied is the base case of the augmented LLM: a single call with retrieval done for it, no planning and no sequencing. A splits a one-step task into three calls and triples cost and latency for no quality gain. B gives the model autonomy to search when the only context it needs has already been provided. C adds coordination overhead to a task that has no independent sub-tasks.

prompt: An architect is choosing between a fixed workflow and an autonomous agent for a new solution. Which TWO properties of the problem most strongly favour the fixed workflow? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The sequence of steps is the same for every request
The number of tool calls varies from one to dozens depending on what intermediate results show
Each step must be individually logged, validated and easy to replay
Requests are open-ended and the right approach is only discovered part-way through the work
The team expects the model to recover from unexpected tool errors by trying alternative approaches

explanation: Correct: A and C. A workflow is the right choice when the path is known up front and when the business needs step-level predictability, validation and replay. B, D and E describe variable, exploratory work where the model must decide its own next step, which is exactly what an agent loop is for.

prompt: A team is deciding whether a merger-screening task justifies a multi-agent design rather than one augmented agent. Which TWO characteristics of the task most strongly indicate that several agents are warranted? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The whole task must finish in under two seconds to meet the agreed response-time target
Legal, financial and technical assessments each need their own tool set and specialist instructions
The task is a single extraction with a fixed schema applied to one document at a time
The assessments can run independently and only need combining at the end
The budget per run is very small and every additional model call must be justified

explanation: Correct: B and D. Multiple agents pay off when sub-tasks need separate context and tools (so one agent's prompt would be bloated and confused) and when they can proceed in parallel and be merged. A and E argue against multi-agent, which adds latency and cost. C is a job for a single call.

prompt: A retailer wants to translate the problem "our returns desk is overwhelmed" into a Claude-based solution. Which TWO activities belong to translating the business problem before any architecture is chosen? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Mapping the current returns process to find where time and errors actually occur
Selecting the embedding model that will be used to index the product catalogue for retrieval
Writing the first version of the system prompt for the returns-desk agent
Choosing between MCP and a direct API integration for connecting to the order system
Defining what a successful outcome looks like and how it will be measured

explanation: Correct: A and E. Translating a business problem means understanding the process as it is and agreeing the measurable outcome; those decide what, if anything, to automate. B, C and D are design and implementation decisions that should follow from that understanding, not precede it.

prompt: A telecoms provider's retention director asks for "a Claude solution to reduce churn". The company already has a well-validated churn-propensity model trained on billing and usage data. What remains poorly understood is why customers leave: the reasons sit in 50,000 free-text cancellation notes and call transcripts a month that nobody reads. How should the architect translate this business problem into a Claude-based solution?

options.text: Replace the existing propensity model by sending each customer's tabular billing and usage history to Claude and asking it for a churn probability
options.explanation: Discards a validated model for a task that tabular machine learning already does well and that is not the actual gap.

options.text: Build an autonomous retention agent that contacts at-risk customers and negotiates discounts, using the propensity score to decide whom to call
options.explanation: Jumps to a high-risk autonomous action without first addressing the stated knowledge gap about reasons for leaving.

options.text: Fine-tune a model on past cancellation notes so that it can generate synthetic transcripts for the retention team to study in workshops
options.explanation: Synthetic transcripts add no insight about real customers and fine-tuning is unnecessary for the analysis that is needed.

options.text: Use Claude to classify and summarise cancellation notes and transcripts into reason codes that feed the retention team and the existing model
options.explanation: Targets Claude at the unstructured-language bottleneck while reusing the validated model for prediction.

explanation: Correct: D. Translating a business problem means locating where language understanding is the real bottleneck; here prediction is solved, but the reasons for churn are locked in unread free text, which Claude can classify and summarise at scale, and the resulting reason codes can enrich the existing model. A swaps a proven tabular model for an LLM on a task it is not best suited to. B adds autonomous customer contact before the insight exists. C produces synthetic data rather than understanding real customers.

prompt: A freight forwarder's pipeline sends scanned bills of lading to Claude, which extracts consignee, weight and port codes into the booking system. Error analysis shows that most wrong extractions come from faded, skewed or partially cropped scans, and on those the model fills gaps with plausible values. Which change to the end-to-end architecture best addresses this?

options.text: Add an input-quality stage before the model that scores each scan and routes unreadable ones to a human queue instead of extraction
options.explanation: Stops bad inputs at the input stage, so the model is never asked to extract from documents it cannot read.

options.text: Add an instruction to the extraction prompt telling the model to be extra careful with difficult documents and to double-check port codes
options.explanation: A prompt exhortation does not make an illegible scan legible and leaves the guessing behaviour largely intact.

options.text: Switch the extraction step to the most capable model available and raise the output token limit so it can reason at greater length
options.explanation: A stronger model still cannot recover information that is physically missing from the image, at higher cost.

options.text: Run the extraction three times per document and keep the most frequent value for each field before writing it to the booking system
options.explanation: Repeated guesses on an unreadable scan can agree with each other and still be wrong, so voting hides the problem.

explanation: Correct: A. End-to-end design covers the input stage as well as processing: when failures originate in unusable inputs, the right control is a gate that detects them and diverts them to a human, rather than asking the model to do the impossible. B relies on wording that cannot fix missing pixels. C spends more on a model that faces the same missing information. D applies voting, which improves consistency but not correctness when every run is guessing.

prompt: An online retailer uses Claude to enrich product listings with attributes such as material, care instructions and size category, and writes the results straight into its product information system. A handful of malformed entries each week have broken storefront filters and displayed impossible values. Which addition to the output stage is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask the model in the prompt to always return valid values and to avoid inventing attributes that are not in the supplier data
options.explanation: Instructions reduce errors but give no enforcement point before bad data reaches the storefront.

options.text: Validate every output against a schema and business rules before writing, and send failing items to a review queue
options.explanation: Creates an enforcement point between model output and the system of record, with a path for exceptions.

options.text: Let the storefront team correct broken listings by hand whenever customers report an obviously impossible attribute value
options.explanation: Reactive manual repair lets defects reach customers first and does not scale with catalogue size.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature for the enrichment calls so that the model produces more deterministic and repeatable attributes
options.explanation: More repeatable output can still be repeatably invalid, so this does not protect the downstream system.

explanation: Correct: B. In an end-to-end architecture the output stage should check model output before it reaches a system of record: schema and rule validation catches malformed or impossible values, and a review queue handles the exceptions. A is useful but unenforced. C detects problems only after customers see them. D affects variability, not validity, so invalid values can still be written.

prompt: A SaaS company wants an in-app help assistant. Each question needs relevant passages from the product documentation and, sometimes, a single read-only lookup of the user's plan. The answer is produced in one turn, and there is no multi-step task to plan. Which architectural pattern is the best starting point?

options.text: An orchestrator-workers design in which a lead model splits each question into sub-questions handled by worker models
options.explanation: Adds orchestration overhead for questions that do not need to be decomposed.

options.text: An autonomous agent that plans its own steps in a loop and decides when it has gathered enough to answer the user
options.explanation: Open-ended autonomy adds cost, latency and unpredictability that a one-turn answer does not need.

options.text: An evaluator-optimiser loop in which a second model critiques each draft answer until it meets a quality rubric
options.explanation: Iterative refinement suits outputs with clear improvement criteria, not routine single-turn help answers.

options.text: An augmented LLM: a single model call given the retrieved documentation and access to the plan lookup as a tool
options.explanation: The simplest pattern that meets the need: retrieval and one tool around a single model call.

explanation: Correct: D. Anthropic's guidance is to start with the simplest pattern that works; the augmented LLM, a model enhanced with retrieval and tools, covers a one-turn answer grounded in documentation plus an occasional lookup. A, B and C are legitimate patterns, but each adds calls, latency and failure modes for benefits this problem does not need: A decomposition, B open-ended planning, and C iterative critique.

prompt: A video platform uses Claude to decide whether user-uploaded descriptions breach its harassment policy. A single classification call is right most of the time, but on borderline items its decisions flip between runs, and wrongly removing content is costly to creator trust. The team wants a more reliable decision on each item. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: Sectioning: split each description into sentences and classify each sentence in parallel, removing the item if any sentence is flagged
options.explanation: Sentence-level splitting loses context that harassment judgements depend on and raises false removals.

options.text: Prompt chaining: first summarise the description, then classify the summary, then write a justification for the decision
options.explanation: Chaining adds steps but still rests on one judgement per item, so borderline instability remains.

options.text: Routing: send each description to a different specialised prompt depending on the language in which it was written
options.explanation: Routing handles distinct input categories; it does not stabilise a judgement on a single borderline item.

options.text: Voting: run several independent classifications of the same item and remove it only when a set threshold of them agree
options.explanation: Multiple independent judgements with a threshold give a more confident, tunable decision on borderline items.

explanation: Correct: D. Voting is the parallelisation variant that runs the same task several times to get diverse outputs, and a vote threshold lets the team trade false removals against missed breaches, which suits an unstable borderline judgement. A is sectioning, which splits a task into different parts rather than repeating it, and here destroys context. B still ends in a single judgement. C addresses heterogeneous inputs, not the reliability of one decision.

prompt: A wealth-management firm's client assistant uses one large prompt that both screens each message for requests it must refuse, such as personalised investment advice, and drafts the reply. Screening is sometimes missed when the answer is long, and the compliance team wants to tune the screening rules without touching the answering prompt. Latency must not grow noticeably. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Move the screening rules to the very end of the combined prompt and mark them as the highest priority instruction for the model
options.explanation: Still one call doing two jobs, so screening remains coupled to answering and cannot be tuned separately.

options.text: Run the screening call first and wait for its result before starting the answer call, so that refused messages never reach the answering model
options.explanation: Separates the concerns but adds the full screening latency in series, which the constraint rules out.

options.text: Let the answering model call a screening tool whenever it judges that a message could involve personalised investment advice
options.explanation: Leaves the decision to screen with the model that is already missing cases, so coverage is not assured.

options.text: Run a dedicated screening call in parallel with the answering call, and release the drafted reply only once screening has passed
options.explanation: Sectioning gives each concern focused attention and separate tuning while keeping latency close to one call.

explanation: Correct: D. Running a guardrail check as a separate call in parallel with the main response is the sectioning form of parallelisation: each call attends to one concern, the screening prompt can be tuned independently, and wall-clock time stays near that of a single call because the reply is held until screening passes. A keeps both jobs in one call. B achieves separation but serialises latency. C makes screening optional and model-initiated.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company's literature-review agent runs dozens of searches per question and reads each returned paper in its main conversation. Halfway through long reviews the agent forgets the reviewer's inclusion criteria and repeats searches it already ran, because its context is crowded with raw abstracts and full-text excerpts. Which change best addresses the cause?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so that all of the raw search results and the instructions fit at once
options.explanation: More room postpones the crowding but keeps the main context full of material it mostly does not need.

options.text: Drop the oldest tool results from the conversation whenever the context passes a fixed size, keeping only recent ones
options.explanation: Blind truncation can discard the very findings and criteria the agent needs, and causes repeated searches.

options.text: Copy the inclusion criteria into every tool result so that the model sees them again each time a paper is returned
options.explanation: Repeating instructions treats a symptom and adds even more tokens to an already crowded context.

options.text: Delegate searching and reading to subagents with separate contexts that return condensed findings
options.explanation: Subagent context isolation keeps raw material out of the main context and returns only what matters.

explanation: Correct: D. Subagents work in their own context windows, so the bulky exploration happens there and only condensed findings flow back to the lead agent, which keeps its criteria and progress in view. A merely raises the ceiling on an inefficient design. B loses information indiscriminately. C repeats instructions while leaving the real cause, raw results flooding the main context, untouched.

prompt: A home insurer's chat service uses a triage agent that identifies the customer and the problem, then hands the conversation to a specialist claims agent. Customers complain that after the handoff they are asked again for their policy number, the incident date and what happened. The specialist agent receives only the customer's latest message. What should the architect change?

options.text: Merge the triage and claims agents into a single agent so that no handoff between separate agents is needed at all
options.explanation: Removes the symptom by giving up the specialisation and scoped tools that motivated the split.

options.text: Give the claims agent the triage agent's full raw transcript, including all its tool calls and intermediate reasoning
options.explanation: Fixes the gap but floods the specialist with noise that its narrow role does not require.

options.text: Define a structured handoff payload with verified identity, collected fields, a short summary and the open request
options.explanation: Passes exactly the state the specialist needs in a predictable form, so nothing is asked twice.

options.text: Tell the claims agent in its system prompt to avoid asking the customer for information they have already provided
options.explanation: The specialist cannot honour this because it never receives the information in the first place.

explanation: Correct: C. Handoffs between agents need an explicit contract: a structured payload carrying verified identity, gathered fields, a summary and the outstanding request gives the specialist the state it needs without the noise. A abandons the benefits of specialisation. B transfers the information but also all of the triage agent's clutter, hurting focus and cost. D instructs the specialist to use information that the architecture never delivers to it.

prompt: A private-equity firm runs due diligence with an orchestrator and five parallel worker agents (financial, legal, commercial, technology, ESG). All workers read and write one shared findings document. Reviewers find sections silently overwritten, contradictory statements left side by side, and no way to tell which worker wrote which claim. What is the best change to how shared state is handled?

options.text: Give each worker its own attributed output store, and make the orchestrator the sole merger and resolver of conflicts
options.explanation: Removes concurrent writes, keeps provenance per claim, and gives conflict resolution a single owner.

options.text: Add a lock so that only one worker can edit the shared document at a time, and keep the rest of the design unchanged
options.explanation: Prevents simultaneous edits but still lets later workers overwrite earlier ones and leaves provenance unclear.

options.text: Run the five workers one after another against the shared document so that each can see and build on earlier sections
options.explanation: Serialising independent work sacrifices parallelism and still leaves later workers free to rewrite earlier findings.

options.text: Instruct every worker in its prompt not to modify text written by other workers and to note any disagreement in a comment
options.explanation: Relies on model compliance for a concurrency and provenance problem that the architecture should prevent.

explanation: Correct: A. Parallel workers should not share a mutable artefact; giving each its own attributed output and making the orchestrator the single writer of the merged report removes overwrites, preserves provenance and places contradiction handling with the component that sees everything. B serialises edits but not ownership, so overwrites and missing attribution remain. C throws away parallelism without fixing ownership. D asks the model to enforce what should be structural.

prompt: A university builds a course-design assistant. The orchestrator launches four subagents at once: one writes learning outcomes, one designs assessments, one drafts the weekly schedule and one compiles the reading list. Results are often inconsistent, for example assessments testing outcomes that were never written and a schedule that ignores the assessments. How should the orchestration be changed?

options.text: Add a fifth subagent that runs at the end and rewrites all four outputs so that they become consistent with each other
options.explanation: Patches inconsistency after the fact and may rewrite good work, instead of fixing the dependency ordering.

options.text: Give each subagent a longer, more detailed prompt describing what the other three subagents are likely to produce
options.explanation: Subagents still cannot see each other's actual output, so guessed assumptions will keep diverging.

options.text: Produce the learning outcomes first, pass them to the steps that depend on them, and parallelise only independent steps
options.explanation: Respects the dependencies so later steps build on real outputs, while keeping parallelism where it is safe.

options.text: Replace the subagents with a vote in which all four produce a complete course design and the most common choices are kept
options.explanation: Voting suits repeated judgements of one task, not assembling interdependent parts of a design.

explanation: Correct: C. Parallelisation is suitable for independent subtasks; when later work depends on earlier outputs, those steps must run in sequence with the outputs passed forward, and only the genuinely independent pieces (for example the reading list) run concurrently. A adds a costly repair pass. B substitutes guesses for real inputs. D applies voting to a problem of dependencies, not of judgement reliability.

prompt: A public-sector team decomposed a planning-application assessment into 28 sequential model calls, one per micro-step such as "extract site address", "extract site area" and "check address format". Latency is high, small errors compound along the chain, and several steps lack the surrounding context they need to judge well. What is the best way to revise the decomposition?

options.text: Collapse all 28 steps back into one large prompt so that the model sees the whole application and every rule at the same time
options.explanation: Swings to the opposite extreme and reintroduces the attention and testability problems decomposition solves.

options.text: Keep all 28 steps but run as many as possible in parallel so that the total latency of the chain is reduced
options.explanation: Most of these steps depend on context or earlier results, so parallelising them worsens the context problem.

options.text: Keep all 28 steps and add a validation model call after each of them to catch errors before they propagate further
options.explanation: Doubles the number of calls and latency while leaving the steps without the context they need.

options.text: Merge tightly coupled micro-steps, and split only where tools, skills or a verifiable intermediate checkpoint differ
options.explanation: Sets step boundaries where they add value, cutting hops and error compounding while keeping checkpoints.

explanation: Correct: D. Good decomposition places boundaries at meaningful seams, such as a change of tool, skill or a point where an intermediate result can be checked, rather than at every micro-action; merging coupled steps restores context and shortens the chain. A overcorrects and loses the benefits of decomposition. B ignores the dependencies between steps. C adds more calls to an already over-fragmented chain without fixing missing context.

prompt: A parcel carrier wants to automate delay notifications. For each delayed shipment the process must parse structured carrier status messages, compute the revised delivery date from route timetables, interpret free-text exception notes written by depot staff, and send the customer a clear, apologetic message. How should the architect decompose the work between Claude and conventional code?

options.text: Use code to parse messages and compute dates; use Claude to interpret depot notes and draft the message
options.explanation: Puts each step with the component best suited to it: deterministic logic in code, language in Claude.

options.text: Use Claude for every step, including timetable arithmetic, so that the whole flow is handled by a single consistent model prompt
options.explanation: Asks a language model to do deterministic arithmetic and parsing that code does more cheaply and reliably.

options.text: Use code for every step, writing keyword rules for depot notes and fixed templates for customer messages to avoid model costs
options.explanation: Keyword rules handle messy free text poorly, which is exactly where language understanding adds value.

options.text: Use Claude to compute the revised dates and interpret the notes, and use code templates to compose the customer messages
options.explanation: Inverts the split: model arithmetic is less reliable, and templates lose the tailored wording needed.

explanation: Correct: A. A key decomposition skill is assigning each subtask to the right mechanism: structured parsing and date arithmetic are deterministic and belong in code, while ambiguous free text and tailored customer wording are where Claude adds value. B wastes tokens and adds error risk on deterministic steps. C forfeits language understanding where the data is messy. D places the model on arithmetic and code on the language task, the reverse of what fits.

prompt: An energy supplier's business case justifies a customer-service assistant under the cost pillar, claiming it will deflect contacts from human agents. The steering group asks for one headline metric that would genuinely evidence that claim after launch. Which should the architect propose?

options.text: The number of conversations the assistant handles each month, compared with the number of conversations in the previous quarter
options.explanation: Volume handled says nothing about cost if many conversations still end with a human contact.

options.text: Fully loaded cost per resolved contact, including inference, platform and escalation costs, against the pre-launch baseline
options.explanation: Measures the cost outcome itself, net of the costs the solution adds and the escalations it causes.

options.text: The average number of tokens per conversation, tracked weekly so that prompt changes can be checked for efficiency gains
options.explanation: A useful engineering signal, but it does not show whether the business is spending less per contact.

options.text: The average customer satisfaction rating given to assistant conversations in the post-chat survey each month
options.explanation: Satisfaction matters but evidences experience quality, not the cost reduction the case claims.

explanation: Correct: B. A value pillar is evidenced by a metric of the outcome it promises; for cost that is the fully loaded cost per resolved contact compared with the baseline, which counts the solution's own running costs and the escalations it fails to deflect. A measures activity, not savings. C is an internal efficiency indicator. D tracks a different dimension, customer experience, rather than cost.

prompt: A health insurer commits to a performance SLA: 99% of prior-authorisation requests must have a draft decision in front of a clinician within two hours of receipt. The proposed agent usually finishes in minutes, but a few cases loop through many record lookups and take far longer. How should the architecture be aligned with the SLA?

options.text: Measure the 99th percentile end to end, give the agent a time and step budget, and route cases that exceed it to a clinician queue
options.explanation: Measures the committed percentile and bounds the tail with a fallback, so slow cases cannot breach the SLA.

options.text: Report the average processing time each week, since the agent finishes most cases in minutes, well inside the two-hour target
options.explanation: An average hides the long tail that the 99% commitment is specifically about.

options.text: Move every case to an overnight batch run to cut costs, and let clinicians pick up all drafts at the start of the next working day
options.explanation: Cheaper processing, but overnight turnaround breaks a two-hour commitment for most requests.

options.text: Switch to the fastest available model for all cases, accepting lower draft quality so that every case finishes within the target
options.explanation: Speeds up calls but does not bound looping cases, and sacrifices quality the clinicians depend on.

explanation: Correct: A. An SLA stated as a percentile needs to be measured as that percentile across the whole journey, and long-tail agent runs need a hard budget with a defined fallback so that the commitment holds even when the agent struggles. B reports a metric that conceals the tail. C optimises cost at the expense of the time commitment. D trades away quality and still leaves runaway loops unbounded.

prompt: An architect is deciding where to use subagents with isolated context windows in a market-intelligence platform. Which TWO situations benefit most from delegating work to subagents with their own contexts? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Exploring many sources produces large volumes of intermediate material, but the lead agent only needs a condensed summary of findings
options.explanation: Isolation keeps bulky exploration out of the lead context and returns compressed results.

options.text: Several agents must edit the same pricing model in tight coordination, each needing to see every change the others make immediately
options.explanation: Tightly coupled work that needs shared live context suffers from isolation and coordination overhead.

options.text: Every step depends on the complete conversation history with the analyst, including the analyst's evolving preferences and corrections
options.explanation: Isolated contexts would lose the shared history that each step relies on.

options.text: A broad question splits into independent sub-questions, such as one per competitor, that can be researched in parallel
options.explanation: Independent breadth-first work parallelises well across separate contexts.

options.text: A simple single lookup of one competitor's stock price must be answered as quickly and cheaply as possible for a dashboard
options.explanation: Spawning subagents adds tokens and latency to a task one call can handle.

explanation: Correct: A and D. Subagents help when their separate context windows compress large exploration into concise results (A) and when a problem breaks into independent threads that can run in parallel (D). B and C describe tightly coupled work or work that needs the full shared history, which multi-agent designs handle poorly because each subagent sees only what it is given. E is a trivial task where subagents add cost and latency for no benefit.

prompt: A bank's operations team is agreeing a service-level agreement for a Claude-based service that triages incoming trade-finance documents for downstream teams. Which TWO items belong in the performance SLA? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An end-to-end latency target per document at a stated percentile, measured at the service boundary
options.explanation: A percentile target at the boundary reflects what downstream teams actually experience.

options.text: A minimum triage accuracy measured on a regularly refreshed, labelled sample of production documents
options.explanation: Quality is part of performance and needs a defined, measurable threshold on real traffic.

options.text: The specific prompt wording and the number of examples that the triage prompt must contain at all times
options.explanation: Implementation details belong in design documents, not in an outcome-based SLA.

options.text: The model provider's published benchmark scores for the model version the service currently uses in production
options.explanation: Generic benchmarks do not measure this service's performance on its own documents.

options.text: The number of agents and tools in the architecture, capped so that the design cannot grow over time
options.explanation: Architecture size is an internal design choice, not a service outcome customers can hold the team to.

explanation: Correct: A and B. A performance SLA should state measurable outcomes that consumers of the service experience: latency at a percentile measured end to end (A), and a quality threshold measured on labelled samples of real traffic (B). C and E fix implementation details that the team must remain free to change. D cites external benchmarks that do not reflect how the service performs on trade-finance documents.

prompt: A claims-handling assistant drafts settlement letters that adjusters review and edit before sending. The architect is designing the feedback loop so that the solution improves over time in a controlled way. Which TWO elements best close that loop? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Retain every raw prompt and response for several years in cold storage, without any link to what the adjuster did next
options.explanation: Storage alone, without outcome data, gives nothing to learn from.

options.text: Let the assistant rewrite its own system prompt automatically each night based on the adjusters' thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings
options.explanation: Uncontrolled self-modification bypasses evaluation and can silently regress behaviour.

options.text: Capture each adjuster's edits and override reasons, linked to the trace of the draft that the assistant produced
options.explanation: Links real outcomes to specific outputs, giving actionable signal about where drafts fall short.

options.text: Add representative failures from reviewed cases to the regression evaluation set run before any prompt or model change
options.explanation: Turns production lessons into tests that gate future changes, so improvements are controlled.

options.text: Build a dashboard of uptime, request volume and token spend, reviewed by the platform team in its weekly operations meeting
options.explanation: Operational health metrics say nothing about whether the drafts are good.

explanation: Correct: C and D. A controlled feedback loop captures outcome signal tied to specific outputs (C) and feeds it back into the evaluation set that gates future changes (D), so the system improves without regressing. A stores data without outcomes. B closes the loop without any evaluation gate, risking silent regressions. E monitors operations rather than output quality.

prompt: A telecom classifies 600,000 short support messages a day into ten intents. On a labelled test set the smallest, middle and largest Claude models score within one point of each other, and the business cares about cost and latency. Which choice is best?

options.text: The largest model, because headroom for the occasional harder message justifies the extra cost
Alternate between the models on each request so that the average cost and latency even out
The middle model, as a reasonable compromise between capability and cost for a production system
The smallest model, since accuracy is equivalent on this task and it is the cheapest and fastest

explanation: Correct: D. Model selection is a trade-off driven by measured task performance: when evaluation shows no accuracy gap, the smaller model wins on both cost and latency at this volume. A pays for capability the data says is not needed. C compromises on a choice the evidence has already made. B adds variance in behaviour and latency for no benefit.

prompt: A legal-drafting feature needs to follow a 30-page playbook, reason about exceptions, and produce long documents, and it runs a few hundred times a day. The team is comparing the most capable Claude model with a mid-tier one. What should drive the decision?

options.text: Choose the mid-tier model as a rule; the capability difference rarely matters for drafting work in practice
Choose whichever model has the larger context window, since the playbook is 30 pages long
Run both on a representative evaluation set and weigh the quality gap against cost at this volume
Choose the most capable model, because legal drafting is important and errors are costly

explanation: Correct: C. The decision is an evidence-based trade-off: measure the quality gap on real examples, then decide whether it is worth the extra cost and latency at a few hundred runs a day, where the absolute cost difference is small. A and D decide on a rule of thumb instead of data. B picks on a dimension that may not differ between the candidates and does not measure the thing that matters.

prompt: An application's system prompt begins with the current date and time and the user's session ID, followed by 11,000 tokens of unchanging product policy, then the user turn. Prompt caching is enabled with a cache breakpoint after the policy, yet cache hits are almost zero. Why?

options.text: The policy section is too large to be cached in one block and must be split into smaller blocks
Caching matches an exact prefix, and the changing timestamp and session ID make every prefix unique
Cache hits only occur when the user message is identical between two consecutive requests
The cache breakpoint must be placed at the very start of the prompt rather than after the policy section

explanation: Correct: B. Prompt caching reuses a prefix that matches exactly up to the breakpoint. Dynamic values placed before the static content change the prefix on every request, so nothing is reusable; moving the timestamp and session ID after the policy (or into the user turn) restores hits. A is backwards: large static blocks are what caching is for. C is wrong because the user turn comes after the breakpoint and does not affect the cached prefix. D would cache nothing useful.

prompt: A team applied chain-of-thought prompting to every endpoint. A multi-step risk-assessment feature improved noticeably, but a simple endpoint that extracts an order number from a message is now slower and costlier with the same accuracy. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep chain-of-thought on every endpoint for consistency across the platform's prompts
Remove chain-of-thought from the risk assessment as well, since it adds cost and latency there too
Keep chain-of-thought for the reasoning-heavy feature and use a direct prompt for the extraction
Replace chain-of-thought with few-shot examples on every endpoint, which are cheaper to run

explanation: Correct: C. Prompting techniques are chosen per task: step-by-step reasoning helps where there are steps to reason through, and is pure overhead on a lookup-style extraction. A pays for reasoning the extraction task does not use. B throws away a measured improvement. D changes technique uniformly again instead of matching technique to task.

prompt: A system prompt holds a non-negotiable rule ("do not disclose wholesale prices") in the middle of 14,000 tokens of product reference material. The rule is followed inconsistently, and rewording it has not helped. Which change is most likely to fix it?

options.text: Repeat the rule three times at different points inside the product reference material
Move the rule into a short delimited instructions section at the top, and restate it after the reference material
Raise the temperature so that the model weighs all parts of the prompt more evenly
Rely on each caller to include the rule in their own message so that it is the most recent instruction

explanation: Correct: B. Structure matters: instructions buried inside long reference content get diluted. Separating instructions from data with clear delimiters, placing critical rules prominently and restating them near the end is the standard structural fix. A adds noise without clear structure. C increases randomness, not adherence. D makes a system-level guardrail depend on each caller including it and leaves it exposed to user-side manipulation.

prompt: A reporting feature must emit output in an exact house format: fixed section order, named headings and a particular table layout. Prose instructions describing the format get it nearly right but not reliably. Which technique most directly fixes this?

options.text: Include two or three complete example outputs in the exact format as few-shot examples
Ask the model to think step by step about the required format before it starts writing
Switch to a larger model and keep the prose description of the format unchanged
Lower the maximum output tokens so that the model has less room to deviate from the format

explanation: Correct: A. Showing the format is more reliable than describing it: few-shot examples pin down structure, heading names and table layout in a way prose cannot. B helps reasoning tasks, not formatting. C may improve adherence somewhat but leaves the ambiguity of a prose spec in place. D truncates output rather than shaping it.

prompt: An assistant answers questions over a 180,000-token set of engineering standards by placing the whole set in context on every request. Answers about material in the middle of the set are noticeably weaker, and each request is slow and expensive. What is the best remedy?

options.text: Retrieve only the sections relevant to each question and place them, clearly labelled, in context
Keep the full set in context and add an instruction to pay particular attention to the middle sections
Split each request across two calls, each carrying half of the standards, and merge the two answers
Compress the standards by stripping all headings, numbering and whitespace to save tokens

explanation: Correct: A. Context window optimisation means putting the right tokens in, not all of them: retrieval cuts cost and latency and removes the mid-context quality dip by giving the model a focused, labelled set of sections. B instructs around a structural problem. C doubles the calls and still cannot say which half holds the answer. D saves a few tokens while destroying the structure the model uses to locate content.

prompt: Six teams in a company each maintain their own copy of a 2,000-token block of brand voice and compliance instructions inside their prompts. Updates are missed and the copies have drifted. Which prompt-reuse strategy addresses this?

options.text: Have each team shorten its own copy so that there is less text to keep in sync between them
Maintain the block as one versioned shared module that each team's prompt composes in at build time
Move the block into every user message so that the latest version is always the one in use
Fine-tune a company model on the brand voice so that the shared instruction block is no longer needed at all

explanation: Correct: B. Modular prompts treat shared instructions as a single, versioned component composed into each prompt, so one update reaches every team and drift stops. A reduces the size of the problem but not its cause. C still leaves six copies and wastes tokens on every turn. D is a heavyweight route to a maintainability problem and makes future updates slower, not faster.

prompt: An agent must apply a 9,000-token procedure for reconciling bank statements, but only about one request in twenty is a reconciliation. The team currently loads the procedure into every system prompt. Which approach keeps the capability while reducing per-request tokens?

options.text: Package the procedure as a Skill with a short description, loaded in full only when needed
Keep the procedure in every prompt but enable prompt caching so the repeated tokens are cheaper
Summarise the procedure to about 500 tokens and accept the loss of detail on the rare reconciliation request
Ask users to state up front whether their request is a reconciliation so the prompt can be chosen

explanation: Correct: A. Skills use progressive disclosure: the model sees only a brief description of each skill and loads the full instructions when they are relevant, so the 9,000 tokens are paid only on the one request in twenty that needs them. B lowers the price of the waste but still sends the tokens every time and consumes context. C sacrifices the detail a procedure exists to provide. D pushes a routing decision onto users.

prompt: A support assistant must stay within a defined scope and decline anything outside it. The team is designing a system prompt to act as that guardrail. Which design is most robust?

options.text: A single sentence asking the model to be helpful and to stay on topic with the customer
A prompt defining role and scope with examples and a refusal behaviour, plus an output check in code
A list of forbidden keywords in the system prompt that the model must not respond to
A system prompt that warns of penalties if the model strays from the defined support topics in any reply

explanation: Correct: B. A guardrail prompt is specific: role, explicit scope with examples of both sides, a defined refusal behaviour, and a check outside the model because a prompt alone can be talked around. A is too vague to be followed consistently. C is brittle and both over- and under-blocks. D does not change capability or scope and is not a reliable instruction technique.

prompt: A high-volume application has a large, mostly static prompt and rising per-request cost. Which TWO changes most directly cut cost per request without reducing capability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Delete the examples section and rely on the model to infer the required output format on its own
Increase the maximum output tokens on every request so that responses are never cut short
Order the prompt so static content comes first and enable prompt caching on it
Send each request twice to two models and keep whichever response turned out to be cheaper
Route simple requests to a smaller model that evaluation shows performs equally on them

explanation: Correct: C and E. Caching a stable prefix cuts the cost of the repeated tokens, and tiering requests to the smallest model that measurably does the job cuts cost where capability is not needed. A reduces tokens by removing something that was there for quality. B does not reduce input cost and may raise output cost. D doubles cost.

prompt: An architect is reviewing a system prompt that produces inconsistent behaviour. Which TWO practices are most likely to improve instruction adherence? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Write the instructions in as few words as possible, even where that leaves some cases implicit
Use clear delimiters or tags to separate instructions, reference data and examples
Place the most important rule in the middle of the prompt where it is surrounded by supporting context
Raise the temperature so that the model handles varied inputs more flexibly and naturally
Replace vague directives with explicit statements of the desired behaviour and its edge cases

explanation: Correct: B and E. Clear structure (so the model can tell instructions from data) and explicit, specific instructions that cover the edge cases are the two highest-leverage fixes for inconsistency. A leaves cases implicit, which is where inconsistency comes from. C buries the rule. D increases variability.

prompt: A team wants a model to extract three fields from a short delivery note. The task is simple, the fields are unambiguous and the team has no labelled examples yet. Which prompting approach should they try first?

options.text: Zero-shot: a clear instruction naming the three fields and the output format
Chain-of-thought: ask the model to reason at length about the note before extracting
Few-shot: a twenty-example prompt built from synthetic delivery notes written by the team
Free text: ask for a prose summary of the note and parse the three fields out of it in code

explanation: Correct: A. Start simple: a precise zero-shot instruction is usually sufficient for an unambiguous extraction and is the cheapest to run and iterate on; add examples or reasoning only if evaluation shows a gap. B adds latency and tokens for a task with nothing to reason through. C front-loads effort on synthetic data before knowing it is needed. D gives up the model's ability to return the fields directly and adds fragile parsing.

prompt: An insurer's pricing team uses Claude to analyse multi-step reinsurance scenarios. Their prompt tells the model to "think step by step inside <thinking> tags" and then lays out a rigid 20-step script. On the hardest scenarios the answers are still shallow, and the team wants deeper reasoning with controllable cost and latency. Which change should the architect recommend?

options.text: Extend the script to 40 numbered steps so that the model is forced to cover every sub-calculation in one fixed order
options.explanation: A longer prescriptive script adds rigidity, not depth, and gives no control over reasoning cost or latency.

options.text: Turn on the model's built-in thinking, tune its depth setting on an eval set, and swap the rigid script for high-level guidance
options.explanation: Native thinking gives a tunable reasoning phase, and high-level guidance usually beats a step-by-step script.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature on the hard scenarios so that the model explores a much wider range of reasoning paths first
options.explanation: Temperature adds randomness to sampling; it does not make the model reason more thoroughly.

options.text: Move all of the reasoning into the answer that reviewers read, and remove the separate thinking section from the prompt entirely
options.explanation: This changes where reasoning appears, not how deep it goes, and clutters the deliverable.

explanation: Correct: B. Model-native thinking gives Claude a dedicated reasoning phase whose depth can be tuned (a token budget or an effort level, depending on the model), so the team can trade quality against cost and latency measured on an evaluation set; Anthropic's guidance is that high-level instructions to think thoroughly often outperform a prescriptive step script. A makes the script more rigid without adding depth control. C only adds sampling randomness. D relocates the reasoning rather than deepening it.

prompt: An engineering consultancy asks Claude questions about tender packs of roughly 60,000 tokens. The current prompt opens with the question and instructions, then pastes all the tender documents as one undifferentiated block. Answers are sometimes vague and mix up which document a requirement came from. Which restructuring is most likely to help?

options.text: Put the documents first, each in a <document> tag with its source, put the question last, and ask for supporting quotes first
options.explanation: Long material above the query, per-document tags with metadata and quote-first grounding are recommended long-context practice.

options.text: Keep the question at the top and restate it in capital letters so the model treats it as the highest-priority part of the prompt
options.explanation: Emphasis does not fix the ordering or the missing document boundaries that cause the mix-ups.

options.text: Strip all of the document headers and merge the files into one block so that the model reads the pack as a single specification
options.explanation: Removing boundaries and sources makes attribution errors more likely, not less.

options.text: Send each question ten times, each with a random tenth of the pack, and return whichever of the ten answers turns out longest
options.explanation: Random partitions split related material, and answer length is not a measure of correctness.

explanation: Correct: A. Anthropic's long-context guidance is to place long documents near the top with the query and instructions at the end, to wrap each document in its own tags with source metadata, and to ask the model to extract relevant quotes before answering; together these improve focus and attribution. B adds emphasis without fixing structure. C removes the very boundaries needed to attribute requirements. D fragments the context and selects answers by an irrelevant criterion.

prompt: An internal HR policy assistant sends a 9,000-token stable prefix with a cache breakpoint after it. Usage is light: requests arrive roughly every 10 to 20 minutes through the working day. Monitoring shows almost every request pays for a cache write and very few get cache reads, so caching is costing more than it saves. What is the most appropriate change?

options.text: Add three more cache breakpoints inside the prefix so that it is cached as several smaller segments that can be reused separately
options.explanation: More breakpoints do not help when every entry has already expired before the next request arrives.

options.text: Use the one-hour cache lifetime on the stable prefix, because the gaps between requests exceed the default five-minute lifetime
options.explanation: The default entry expires between requests; a one-hour lifetime keeps the prefix warm across the observed gaps.

options.text: Move the cache breakpoint to the end of the user message so that each complete request is stored and reused by later requests
options.explanation: The user message differs every time, so caching it adds writes that are never read.

options.text: Turn caching off entirely, since prompt caching only pays off for applications that receive many requests in every second
options.explanation: Caching pays off whenever reuse falls within the lifetime; a longer lifetime fits this traffic pattern.

explanation: Correct: B. The default cache lifetime is five minutes, refreshed each time the entry is read; with gaps of 10 to 20 minutes the entry expires and every request pays a write premium. The one-hour lifetime costs more to write but turns most requests into reads for this traffic. A adds segments that expire just the same. C caches content that never repeats. D gives up a saving that is available once the lifetime matches the request cadence.

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS agent sends the same 6,000-token system prompt on every request, with a cache breakpoint after it. To enforce plan entitlements, the application builds the `tools` array per request, including only the tools the tenant's plan allows and stamping the tenant's name into each tool description. Cache reads on the system prompt are near zero. What is the cause, and the best fix?

options.text: The system prompt is too large to cache in one piece; split it across several breakpoints so that each part fits within the limit
options.explanation: There is no such upper limit problem here; the prefix differs before the system prompt is even reached.

options.text: Cache entries are scoped to one tenant at a time; switch to the one-hour lifetime so that each tenant's entry lasts between visits
options.explanation: Tenancy is not the cause; the per-request tools array changes the prefix, so a longer lifetime still misses.

options.text: Tools come before the system prompt in the cached prefix; send one stable tool set and enforce entitlements in the tools' handlers
options.explanation: Changing tool definitions invalidates everything after them; entitlements belong in code below the model anyway.

options.text: Caching ignores the tools array entirely; add a further breakpoint on the last user message so that the history is cached as well
options.explanation: Tools are part of the cached prefix, and a later breakpoint cannot hit when the earlier prefix differs.

explanation: Correct: C. The cached prefix is built in the order tools, system, messages, and a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it, so per-tenant tool arrays and tenant names in descriptions defeat the system-prompt cache. A stable tool set with authorisation enforced in the tool handlers restores hits and is the sounder security design. A misdiagnoses a size issue. B blames tenancy, but the prefix itself differs. D is wrong because tools are part of the prefix.

prompt: A university's learning-technology team wrote a Skill for grading lab reports against a rubric. Its frontmatter description reads "Lab report helper". The detailed guidance on when to apply it lives in the SKILL.md body, and the rubric sits in a bundled reference file. In testing, Claude rarely uses the Skill even when staff ask it to grade lab reports. What should the team change?

options.text: Move the rubric and every bundled reference file into the SKILL.md body so that Claude sees all of the material from the very start
options.explanation: The SKILL.md body is only read after the Skill triggers, so this does not help it trigger and bloats it.

options.text: Rewrite the description to say what the Skill does and when to use it, since only name and description are seen before it loads
options.explanation: Before triggering, only the metadata is in context, and the description is what requests are matched against.

options.text: Paste the whole SKILL.md and the rubric into the system prompt of every conversation so the grading guidance is always present
options.explanation: This works around the problem by abandoning progressive disclosure and paying the token cost on every request.

options.text: Convert the rubric file into an executable script, because Claude only triggers Skills that contain at least one runnable script
options.explanation: Scripts are optional resources; triggering depends on the description, not on whether code is bundled.

explanation: Correct: B. Skills use progressive disclosure: only each Skill's name and description are loaded at startup, the SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill is triggered, and bundled files or scripts are read or run only as needed. A vague description gives Claude nothing to match a grading request against. A edits content that is not visible until after triggering. C defeats the token savings Skills exist to provide. D rests on a false premise about scripts.

prompt: A logistics company's route-planning agent makes hundreds of tool calls per session, reading large depot schedules and carrier rate files. Late in long runs it slows down, costs climb and it eventually hits the context limit, even though most old tool results are no longer needed once processed. A few findings from early files are needed again much later. Which approach best sustains long runs?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window and keep every tool result in the history so that nothing processed earlier is lost
options.explanation: This postpones the limit while cost and latency keep growing with every stale result carried forward.

options.text: Truncate every tool result to its first 200 characters as soon as it returns, before the agent has had a chance to read it fully
options.explanation: The agent loses data it has not yet processed, which harms planning quality.

options.text: Clear the oldest tool results past a context threshold, and have the agent note its key findings in a memory file it can re-read
options.explanation: Clearing stale results bounds context, and the memory file preserves the few facts needed later.

options.text: Restart the agent with an empty context whenever it nears the limit and let it redo whatever work it had already completed before
options.explanation: Restarting discards progress and repeats tool calls, raising cost instead of cutting it.

explanation: Correct: C. Context editing that clears the oldest tool results past a threshold removes material the agent has already processed, and pairing it with a memory file (or a summary via compaction) keeps the few findings that matter later, so long runs stay within budget. A treats capacity as the fix while cost keeps climbing. B discards data before it is used. D throws away progress and repeats work.

prompt: A travel-booking platform uses Claude to handle customer change requests. About 85% are routine date changes; the rest involve multi-leg itineraries, fare rules and partner airlines. Running everything on the most capable model meets quality targets but is too slow and expensive at peak. Which design best balances cost, latency and quality?

options.text: Run every request on the smallest model and retry each failed request up to five times, since retries cost less than a bigger model
options.explanation: Blind retries do not supply missing capability for complex cases and add latency to them.

options.text: Route routine requests to a smaller model and escalate complex or failed-check cases to the larger one, validated by evaluation
options.explanation: Tiering by difficulty spends capability only where needed, with evaluation confirming each tier holds quality.

options.text: Let customers pick a fast model or a thorough model in the interface, leaving the choice and the whole trade-off entirely to them
options.explanation: Customers cannot judge which model their request needs; this pushes an architectural decision onto users.

options.text: Keep the largest model for every request but halve the maximum output length so that each of the responses is cheaper and quicker
options.explanation: Capping output risks truncated answers and leaves input cost and model latency largely unchanged.

explanation: Correct: B. Model tiering routes the routine majority to a smaller, faster model and escalates complex requests, or those that fail a validation check, to the more capable model, with evaluation confirming each tier meets the quality bar. A relies on retries that cannot add capability. C hands an engineering trade-off to customers who lack the information to make it. D trims output length, which risks truncation without addressing the main cost and latency driver.

prompt: A media company summarises podcast transcripts that range from a few thousand to several hundred thousand tokens. The pipeline estimates size by dividing character count by four; some requests fail for exceeding the context window, while others are chunked unnecessarily. What should the team do?

options.text: Lower the assumed characters-per-token ratio to two so that the estimate is always conservative and no request ever overflows
options.explanation: A cruder heuristic still mis-estimates and would chunk far more transcripts than necessary.

options.text: Send every transcript as it is, catch the error, then chunk and resend only those requests that the API rejects as too long
options.explanation: Using failures as the size check wastes calls and latency when the size can be measured beforehand.

options.text: Split every transcript into fixed 10,000-token chunks whatever its length, so that no request ever comes near the context limit
options.explanation: Chunking short transcripts needlessly fragments them and adds extra merge steps.

options.text: Count tokens with the token-counting endpoint first, and chunk only if that count plus the expected output exceeds the window
options.explanation: Measuring tokens directly avoids both overflows and needless chunking.

explanation: Correct: D. The token-counting endpoint returns the input token count for a prospective request, including system prompt and tools, so the pipeline can decide accurately whether a transcript plus room for output fits before sending it. A swaps one heuristic for another and over-chunks. B uses errors as a measurement tool, wasting calls. C chunks every transcript regardless of need, fragmenting the short ones.

prompt: A retail bank runs a dozen customer-letter prompts that differ only in product name, applicable rules and the customer's details, but each was hand-edited separately and they have drifted apart. The architect wants one maintainable, testable approach that also keeps customer data clearly separated from instructions. Which design fits best?
