options.text: Merge all twelve prompts into one large prompt covering every product, and let the model work out which sections apply each time
options.explanation: One sprawling prompt dilutes relevant instructions and makes changes for one product risky for all.

options.text: Have each team keep its own prompt but circulate edits to the others weekly, so that changes spread across the variants over time
options.explanation: Manual propagation is what caused the drift; it does not create a single source of truth.

options.text: Splice the customer's details straight into the instruction sentences wherever they are needed, so that the prompt reads naturally
options.explanation: Mixing data into instructions blurs the boundary the architect wants and invites instruction confusion.

options.text: Build one versioned template with the fixed instructions first and variables like {{product}} and {{customer}} wrapped in XML tags
options.explanation: A template gives one source of truth, tagged variables separate data, and a static prefix suits caching.

explanation: Correct: D. A single version-controlled template keeps the fixed instructions in one place and fills product and customer variables at run time; wrapping variables in XML tags separates data from instructions, and putting static content first also makes the prefix cacheable and the template testable against an evaluation set. A creates a bloated catch-all prompt. B is the manual process that caused the drift. C merges data into instructions, the opposite of the stated goal.

prompt: A hospital is building a discharge-summary assistant. The architect must decide where to place the assistant's role as a clinical documentation aide and its standing rules, and where to place each patient's notes and the specific summary request. Which placement follows recommended practice?

options.text: Put the role, standing rules, patient notes and request all in the system prompt, leaving the user turn empty on each call
options.explanation: Per-request data and tasks belong in the user turn; stuffing them into the system prompt also defeats reuse and caching.

options.text: Set the role and standing rules in the system prompt, and pass the patient's notes and the specific request in the user turn
options.explanation: The system prompt carries the stable role and rules; task-specific content goes in the user turn.

options.text: Leave out the role entirely, since giving Claude a role changes only its tone and has no effect on accuracy in specialist domains
options.explanation: Role prompting can improve focus and domain performance, not just tone.

options.text: Put the role and rules in the user turn of every request and keep the system prompt empty so that there is less for the model to read
options.explanation: Repeating stable rules per turn gains nothing and loses the system prompt's role-setting purpose.

explanation: Correct: B. Anthropic recommends using the system prompt to set Claude's role and the stable rules that apply to every request, and putting task-specific instructions and data, here the patient's notes and the summary request, in the user turn. A puts changing data into the system prompt. C underrates role prompting, which can improve domain accuracy. D moves stable rules out of the place designed for them without reducing what the model reads.

prompt: A retailer extracts product attributes from supplier descriptions into JSON consumed by an inventory service. The legacy design prefilled the assistant turn with an opening brace, but the model version the team is moving to does not accept a prefilled final assistant turn. Without it, responses occasionally include a preamble or invalid JSON that breaks the parser. Which approach is most reliable?

options.text: Use structured outputs, or a tool whose input schema defines the attributes, so responses are constrained to the schema
options.explanation: Schema-constrained output removes preambles and malformed JSON at the source.

options.text: Stay on the older model version indefinitely so the prefill keeps working, and postpone the migration until it is finally retired
options.explanation: This defers the problem and forgoes the newer model's improvements without fixing the format.

options.text: Add a sentence in capital letters telling the model it must output only JSON, and log any failures for the team to repair by hand
options.explanation: Stronger wording reduces but does not eliminate format errors, and manual repair does not scale.

options.text: Strip everything before the first brace with a regular expression and accept that occasional malformed objects will be dropped
options.explanation: Post-processing hides preambles but silently loses records when the JSON itself is invalid.

explanation: Correct: A. When output must parse, constrain it: structured outputs with a JSON schema, or a tool whose input schema defines the attributes, makes valid schema-shaped JSON the response format instead of hoping the model complies. B blocks migration without solving the underlying problem. C relies on emphasis and manual clean-up. D treats the symptom and silently drops data whenever the JSON is invalid.

prompt: An energy retailer's support agent sends tool definitions, a long instruction block, a knowledge-base section refreshed every hour, and a growing conversation history on each turn. Cache hit rates are disappointing. Which TWO design choices most improve cache reuse? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Order content from most to least stable with separate breakpoints, so a knowledge-base refresh leaves tools and instructions cached
options.explanation: A change invalidates only its own segment and those after it, so stable segments placed first stay cached.

options.text: Insert the current timestamp at the start of the instruction block so that the model always knows exactly how fresh the knowledge base is
options.explanation: A changing value early in the prefix invalidates everything after it on every request.

options.text: Use a single breakpoint at the very start of the prompt so that the cache covers the whole request without further configuration
options.explanation: A breakpoint caches the prefix up to that point; placing it at the start caches almost nothing.

options.text: Send only the tools relevant to each turn, adding and removing tool definitions as the conversation moves between topics
options.explanation: Tool definitions head the prefix, so changing them each turn invalidates the entire cache.

options.text: Keep settings such as tool choice and the thinking configuration constant across turns, as changes invalidate cached messages
options.explanation: These settings are part of the cache key for message blocks, so varying them forces fresh cache writes.

explanation: Correct: A and E. The cache follows the hierarchy tools, system, messages, and a change invalidates its own level and everything after it, so ordering content by stability with breakpoints between segments lets an hourly knowledge-base refresh leave tools and instructions cached (A); changing tool choice or the thinking configuration invalidates cached message blocks, so they should stay constant (E). B puts a changing value early in the prefix. C caches almost nothing. D changes the first level of the prefix every turn.

prompt: A government benefits agency classifies incoming letters into 15 case types. Zero-shot results confuse several similar types, so the team is adding few-shot examples to the prompt. Which TWO practices should guide how they write the examples? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choose examples that vary in wording, length and case type, including the confusable pairs, so the model does not copy one pattern
options.explanation: Diverse, relevant examples covering the hard distinctions teach the boundary rather than a surface pattern.

options.text: Use one example repeated with minor wording changes, so that the model sees one consistent pattern it can match with high confidence
options.explanation: Near-identical examples encourage overfitting to one pattern and teach nothing about the confused types.

options.text: Wrap each example in <example> tags so it stays clearly separated from the instructions and from the letter being classified
options.explanation: Tagging examples keeps them distinct from instructions and live input, reducing confusion.

options.text: Pick examples only from the most common case type, since those are the letters the model will see most often in production traffic
options.explanation: Examples from one type do nothing to resolve confusion between the similar, less common types.

options.text: Let the examples quietly contradict the written rules where convenient, because the model will follow the instructions over examples
options.explanation: Models weigh examples heavily, so contradictions with the rules produce inconsistent behaviour.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Anthropic's guidance is that few-shot examples should be relevant and diverse, covering edge cases and the distinctions the model gets wrong so it does not latch onto an unintended pattern (A), and wrapped in <example> tags so they are kept apart from instructions and input (C). B and D make the examples narrow, which teaches nothing about the confusable types. E creates conflicting signals, and examples strongly influence output.

prompt: A company is connecting Claude to fifteen internal systems owned by different teams. Tools will be added and retired often, and several AI applications across the company need the same integrations. Which integration approach best fits?

options.text: Each application embeds its own direct API client for every one of the systems it needs
Applications call one another's agents to borrow the integrations they do not have themselves
One central team writes a single library containing all fifteen integrations and ships it to every application
Each system team publishes an MCP server for its system, and applications connect to the ones they need

explanation: Correct: D. MCP is designed for exactly this: a standard protocol in which each system is exposed once, by the team that owns it, and any number of model applications can discover and use it. A multiplies integration work by the number of applications. C centralises ownership away from the teams that know the systems and creates a release bottleneck. B couples applications to each other for no architectural reason.

prompt: An agent has grown to 52 registered tools across seven business areas. Tool-selection accuracy has fallen, latency has risen, and usage logs show that 20 of the tools have never been called in production. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Remove the unused tools, then group the rest so each request sees only its area's tools
Add more detailed descriptions to all 52 tools so that the model can tell them apart more reliably
Raise the model's maximum output tokens so that it can reason for longer about which tool to use
Move to the largest model available, which handles large tool sets more accurately than smaller ones

explanation: Correct: A. This is capability bloat: every registered tool costs tokens and dilutes selection on every call, so prune what is unused and scope what remains. B improves descriptions on tools that should not be there at all. C and D spend money on symptoms while the tool list keeps growing.

prompt: An assistant answers employees' questions about their own payroll records. It calls the payroll API with one service account that can read every employee's data, and the system prompt tells the model to return only the asking employee's records. A security review flags this. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Add a second instruction to the system prompt forbidding access to any other employee's data
Log every payroll query with the asking employee's ID so that any misuse can be detected and investigated afterwards
Pass the authenticated employee's identity to the tool layer and let the payroll API enforce the scope
Switch to a model that follows system-prompt instructions more reliably under adversarial input

explanation: Correct: C. Authorization must be enforced below the model, in the tool or API layer, using the caller's real identity; a prompt is not an access-control mechanism and can be manipulated. A and D keep the control in the prompt, which is the gap the review found. B is a detective control that catches disclosure after it has happened.

prompt: An HR onboarding agent was built on a generic "people operations" MCP server that exposes tools to view records, edit records, change salaries and terminate employment. The onboarding team only ever views and edits records. Applying least privilege, what should change?

options.text: Keep the full tool set but require a manager's confirmation before salary changes and terminations
Keep the full tool set and write every salary change and termination to an immutable audit log
Connect the agent only to the view and edit tools, leaving the other two unavailable to it
Add a system-prompt rule stating that the salary and termination tools must never be used by this agent

explanation: Correct: C. Least privilege means not granting a capability the role does not need; scoping the agent to the two tools it uses removes the risk rather than guarding it. A and B are compensating and detective controls that leave the dangerous capability in place. D relies on the model to decline a tool it has been given, which an injection or a mistake can override.

prompt: A RAG system over supplier contracts splits every document into fixed 250-token chunks. Retrieved chunks are often clause fragments whose meaning depends on definitions and cross-references elsewhere in the contract, and answers suffer. Which chunking change addresses this?

options.text: Reduce the chunks to 100 tokens so that retrieval becomes more precise about the matching clause
Chunk along clauses and sections, add overlap, and prepend document and section context to each chunk
Index each whole contract as a single chunk so that no clause is ever separated from its definitions
Keep the 250-token chunks but retrieve the top 50 instead of the top 5 so the context is more complete

explanation: Correct: B. Chunking should follow the shape of the data: structure-aware chunks with overlap and contextual headers keep a clause intact and tell the model which contract and section it came from. A makes the fragments smaller and worse. C produces chunks too large to retrieve precisely or fit several of in context. D floods the context with fragments instead of fixing them.

prompt: A spare-parts assistant uses purely semantic vector retrieval. Natural-language questions work well, but searches for exact part codes such as "TR-7731-C" often return similar-looking but wrong parts. Which retrieval strategy fixes this?

options.text: Replace the vector retrieval with keyword search only, since part codes are the harder case
Increase the embedding dimension so that codes like "TR-7731-C" are represented more precisely
Ask users to describe the part in words instead of entering codes, which embeddings handle well already
Hybrid retrieval: combine the semantic index with a lexical index so exact identifiers match

explanation: Correct: D. Retrieval should match the query pattern: embeddings capture meaning but not exact strings, while lexical search matches identifiers precisely, so combining the two serves both query types. A fixes codes but breaks the natural-language queries that currently work. B does not make embeddings exact-match. C works around the problem by changing user behaviour.

prompt: Adding a re-ranking step to a support assistant's retrieval raises answer accuracy from 85% to 92% and adds 600 ms. The contractual response-time SLA is 3 seconds and current p95 latency is 1.5 seconds. What should the architect decide?

options.text: Reject the re-ranker, because any added latency erodes the margin against the contractual SLA
Adopt the re-ranker: the gain is material, p95 stays inside the SLA, and record the decision
Adopt the re-ranker only for requests that arrive outside business hours when traffic is lower
Run the re-ranker asynchronously and update the answer on screen after it has already been shown to the user

explanation: Correct: B. An accuracy-latency trade-off is decided with numbers: a 7-point accuracy gain for 600 ms that leaves p95 at about 2.1 seconds against a 3-second SLA is a clear win, and the justification should be documented. A treats latency as the only metric. C makes quality depend on the clock. D shows users a worse answer first and complicates the experience for no latency reason.

prompt: A platform runs 80,000 agent sessions a day. Engineers log every full prompt, response and tool payload; storage cost is high and failures are still hard to locate. Which observability strategy is more appropriate at this scale?

options.text: Stop logging prompts and responses entirely and keep only aggregate error counts per day
Keep logging every prompt, response and tool payload in full but shorten retention to a single day to cut the storage bill
Structured traces per session with correlation IDs, step metadata, sampled payloads and full capture on failure
Keep full logging but add full-text search and longer retention over the raw payloads

explanation: Correct: C. Observability at scale is about structure and sampling: traces that link every step of a session, metadata you can query, and full payloads only for a sample plus the failures you need to debug. A removes the information needed to diagnose anything. B keeps the cost problem and loses history. D makes the cost problem bigger and still searches raw payloads rather than structured steps.

prompt: A hospital's scheduling agent must coordinate appointment slots with an independently operated transport provider's agent. Neither organisation will expose internal systems or tools to the other. Which connection mechanism fits?

options.text: The hospital agent is given direct API credentials for the transport provider's booking system
The transport provider publishes an MCP server exposing its internal tools for the hospital agent
An agent-to-agent protocol: the two agents exchange structured messages and keep their tools private
A shared database hosted by a third party that both organisations' agents read from and write to directly

explanation: Correct: C. When two autonomous agents under different ownership must cooperate without exposing internals, agent-to-agent communication is the mechanism: each side keeps its tools and systems behind its own agent and they exchange messages at the boundary. A and B expose one organisation's systems to the other's agent, which was ruled out. D is a tighter coupling than either organisation would accept.

prompt: An existing invoice-processing microservice needs to call Claude exactly once per document to classify it, inside its own tightly controlled pipeline with no need for the model to discover tools. Which integration mechanism is the most appropriate?

options.text: A direct Claude API call from the service with the document and the classification instructions
An MCP server wrapping the invoice service so that the model can discover and call it
An autonomous agent with the invoice service's functions registered as tools it may call
An agent-to-agent exchange between the invoice service and a separate classification agent run by another team

explanation: Correct: A. A single, deterministic model call inside existing application code is a direct API integration; MCP and agents add discovery and autonomy that this pipeline does not want. B inverts the direction: the service calls the model, not the other way round. C and D add planning and messaging overhead to a one-shot classification.

prompt: A knowledge agent could either load all 60 tool definitions and 30,000 tokens of reference material into every request, or load a short catalogue and fetch tool definitions and reference sections on demand. Requests are varied and most need two or three tools. Which strategy should the architect choose and why?

options.text: Monolithic context, because fetching on demand adds a round trip that the user would notice on every request
Progressive discovery, because most requests use a small fraction of the material
Monolithic context, because the model performs best when it can see all the tools and material at once
Progressive discovery, because it removes the need to maintain any tool descriptions at all

explanation: Correct: B. With varied requests that each use a small slice of a large tool and context set, progressive discovery wins: smaller prompts, less distraction, better selection, and the added lookup is cheap relative to the tokens saved. A overweights one extra round trip against a 30,000-token prompt. C is the opposite of what happens with large, mostly irrelevant context. D misdescribes the approach: a catalogue of short descriptions is still needed to choose what to load.

prompt: A RAG index is rebuilt nightly from a documentation site. After some rebuilds the assistant quotes superseded pages for part of the day. Which indexing practice addresses this most directly?

options.text: Rebuild the index every hour instead of every night so that superseded pages are replaced much sooner
Build the new index fully, switch to it atomically, and version each chunk's metadata
Instruct the model to prefer the content that sounds most recent whenever two retrieved chunks conflict
Retrieve more chunks per query so that the current version of a page is more likely to be included

explanation: Correct: B. Stale answers after a refresh come from serving a half-updated index or mixing old and new chunks; an atomic swap plus versioned metadata removes both causes. A makes the window of inconsistency more frequent rather than smaller. C asks the model to guess at freshness. D increases the chance of including stale chunks alongside current ones.

prompt: An agent has three tools named `search_docs`, `find_docs` and `lookup_docs` with similar one-line descriptions, and it frequently picks the wrong one. What should the architect change first?

options.text: Merge the overlapping tools and give each a distinct name and a description of when to use it
Add a fourth tool whose only job is to decide which of the three existing search tools should be called
Increase the number of retries so that the agent eventually lands on the right tool for the request
Present the three tools in a random order on each request to avoid any bias toward the first one

explanation: Correct: A. Tool selection is driven by names and descriptions: overlapping tools with vague descriptions are the root cause, so consolidate and describe precisely, including when not to use each. B adds a layer of indirection on top of the ambiguity. C makes errors slower and more expensive rather than rarer. D shuffles a problem it does not solve.

prompt: An internal MCP server exposes a `run_sql` tool that accepts arbitrary SQL against the analytics warehouse. The agent using it only ever needs monthly revenue by region. A security review asks for a change. Which is the best?

options.text: Keep `run_sql` but add a system-prompt rule that only SELECT statements may ever be issued
Replace `run_sql` with a narrow tool such as `revenue_by_region(month)` that runs a read-only query
Keep `run_sql` and log every statement it runs so that any misuse can be reviewed by the security team later
Keep `run_sql` and have the model confirm each query with the user before it is executed

explanation: Correct: B. A tool's interface defines the blast radius: a narrow, parameterised, read-only tool gives the agent exactly the capability it needs and nothing else, and it also improves selection and reliability. A puts a security boundary in the prompt. C detects misuse after the fact. D pushes the control onto the user and slows every request.

prompt: A new internal knowledge base should be usable by any current or future agent in the organisation without each agent team writing its own integration. Which mechanism serves this best?

options.text: A direct API call coded into each agent that needs to read from the knowledge base
A shared system prompt that includes the knowledge base contents for every agent to use
An MCP server for the knowledge base that any agent can connect to and discover
A nightly export of the knowledge base sent to each agent team to load however they prefer

explanation: Correct: C. Exposing a capability once, with discoverable tools and resources, for any model application to use is what MCP is for. A repeats the integration per agent. B does not scale and goes stale. D is not an integration at all.

prompt: A RAG assistant for a field-service company must answer two kinds of query: free-text questions about repair procedures, and lookups of a specific job by job number. Which TWO measures best match retrieval to these query patterns? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a single vector index for both and rely on the model to notice when a match is wrong
Retrieve the top 100 chunks for every query so that the right one is always somewhere in context
Remove job numbers from the index entirely so that they cannot cause confusion in semantic search
Use semantic retrieval for procedure questions and an exact-match lookup for job numbers
Attach metadata such as equipment type and date to chunks so retrieval can filter before ranking

explanation: Correct: D and E. Different query patterns call for different retrieval paths, and metadata filtering narrows the candidate set before semantic ranking. A leaves the exact-identifier weakness in place. B floods the context. C deletes the data needed for the lookup use case.

prompt: An architect is reviewing the authentication design of an agent that calls several internal APIs on behalf of users. Which TWO findings represent security gaps? (Select TWO.)

options.text: API keys for the internal systems are placed in the system prompt so the model can include them in tool calls
The agent acts under one shared service identity regardless of which user is asking
Tool calls are executed by application code that holds the credentials outside the model's context
Each tool call carries the end user's identity and the API enforces that user's own permissions
Credentials are rotated regularly and scoped to the minimum that each individual tool needs

explanation: Correct: A and B. Secrets in the prompt can be leaked in output or by injection, and a single shared identity means the API cannot enforce per-user permissions, so the model becomes the only access control. C, D and E are the correct practices: credentials held outside the model, user identity propagated to the enforcing layer, and least-privilege scoping.

prompt: An architect is weighing progressive discovery (loading tools and context on demand) against a monolithic strategy (everything in context up front). Which TWO situations most strongly favour progressive discovery? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Every request uses the same three tools and a 1,500-token prompt that rarely changes
The system has a hard requirement of exactly one model call per request with no extra lookups
The tool and reference set is large and any single request uses only a small part of it
New tools and documents are added often and must become available without redeploying the prompt
The whole context fits comfortably in the window and is fully covered by prompt caching

explanation: Correct: C and D. Progressive discovery pays off when the full set is large and sparsely used, and when the catalogue changes often, because on-demand loading keeps prompts small and lets new capabilities appear without prompt changes. A and E describe small, stable contexts where monolithic loading is simpler and cheaper. B rules out the extra lookup step that discovery needs.

prompt: A monitoring dashboard for a production agent shows average latency and total token spend per day. The team still cannot tell which step of a failing session went wrong. Which TWO additions would let them? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A correlation ID that links every model call and tool call in a session into one trace
Average latency broken down by model version and by hour of the day
A weekly email summarising total spend and request volume for the engineering managers
Per-step records of tool name, input summary, outcome and duration
Removing tool-call logging altogether to reduce noise in the dashboards and cut storage

explanation: Correct: A and D. Diagnosing a failing session requires tracing: a session-level identifier that ties the steps together, and structured step-level records to inspect. B and C are aggregate reporting that cannot point at a step inside one session. E removes the very data needed.

prompt: A broadcaster is building an MCP server for its news archive. It must offer three things: a publish action that the model decides when to invoke, read-only article texts that the client application attaches to the conversation as context, and editorial templates (such as "write a correction notice") that journalists pick from a menu. How should these map onto MCP server primitives?

options.text: Expose all three as tools, because tools are the one primitive that Claude-based clients can consume, and describe each tool's purpose in its description field
options.explanation: MCP defines resources and prompts alongside tools, and Claude clients can use them; forcing everything into tools hands control of context and templates to the model.

options.text: Expose the article texts as prompts, the editorial templates as resources and the publish action as a tool so that the model controls only the write operation
options.explanation: This swaps two primitives: prompts are user-selected templates and resources are context data managed by the application.

options.text: Expose the publish action as a tool, the article texts as resources and the editorial templates as prompts that the client surfaces for users to choose
options.explanation: Correct: tools are model-controlled actions, resources are application-controlled context, and prompts are user-controlled templates.

options.text: Expose the publish action as a prompt so that a journalist must confirm each use, and expose both the article texts and the templates as resources
options.explanation: Prompts are templates a user invokes, not a confirmation mechanism for actions; approval of a write belongs in the client or tool layer.

explanation: Correct: C. The MCP specification defines three server primitives with different controllers: tools are model-controlled functions that take actions, resources are application-controlled contextual data such as file or article contents, and prompts are user-controlled templates typically surfaced as slash commands or menu items. A wrongly assumes tools are the only usable primitive. B swaps resources and prompts. D misuses prompts as an approval gate; confirmation of a publish action is a client or tool-layer control.

prompt: A project-management SaaS vendor distributes its MCP server as a local package that customers run on their own machines over stdio, each pasting a personal API key into a config file. The vendor now wants to update the server centrally without customers reinstalling it, and wants customers' users to sign in with their existing vendor accounts instead of handling API keys. Which design fits?

options.text: Keep the stdio package but embed one vendor-wide API key in it, so that users need no configuration and updates ship through the normal package manager
options.explanation: A shared embedded key gives every user identical, unrevocable access and still requires reinstallation for updates.

options.text: Keep the stdio package and add an auto-update check at start-up, while continuing to read each user's personal API key from an environment variable
options.explanation: This eases updates but keeps users handling long-lived API keys, which the vendor explicitly wants to remove.

options.text: Host the server remotely over Streamable HTTP and use MCP's OAuth-based authorisation, so that each user signs in and the client gets a scoped token
options.explanation: Correct: a remote HTTP server is updated in one place, and MCP authorisation for HTTP transports is built on OAuth so users sign in rather than manage keys.

options.text: Host the server remotely on a public HTTP endpoint without authentication, giving each customer an unguessable URL that acts as its access credential
options.explanation: An unguessable URL is a bearer secret with no user identity, scoping or revocation, and it leaks easily through logs and sharing.

explanation: Correct: C. A remote MCP server using the Streamable HTTP transport can be updated centrally, and the MCP authorisation specification for HTTP-based transports builds on OAuth, letting each user sign in and the client obtain a token scoped to that user; stdio servers instead typically read credentials from the local environment. A shares one unrevocable key and still needs reinstalls. B fixes updates but keeps users handling API keys. D replaces authentication with a guessable-in-practice shared secret.

prompt: A logistics company's nightly freight-reconciliation agent runs with no user present. It authenticates using the stored refresh token of the operations manager who set it up, so it carries that manager's full permissions across finance and dispatch systems. The manager is leaving the company next month. What should the architect change?

options.text: Re-authorise the agent with the refresh token of the manager's successor before the departure, so that nightly runs continue without interruption
options.explanation: This repeats the flaw: the agent still borrows a person's broad permissions and its actions are still attributed to a human.

options.text: Create one shared administrator account for all scheduled automation jobs, so that staff changes never affect them and credentials live in one place
options.explanation: A shared admin identity maximises privilege and blast radius and makes individual jobs' actions impossible to tell apart.

options.text: Extend the lifetime of the manager's refresh token and store it in the secrets manager, so that it keeps working after the account is deactivated
options.explanation: Keeping a departed employee's credential alive defeats offboarding and leaves an orphaned, over-privileged token in use.

options.text: Give the agent its own non-human workload identity, issued from the secrets manager, with only the scopes that the nightly reconciliation job needs
options.explanation: Correct: an autonomous job should act as itself with least-privilege scopes, so its actions are attributable and survive staff changes.

explanation: Correct: D. An agent that runs without a user should not borrow a person's delegated credentials; it needs its own workload identity scoped to exactly the systems and operations the reconciliation uses, with credentials managed and rotated outside the model. Its actions are then auditable as the agent's, and offboarding staff does not break it. A and C keep a human's broad permissions attached to the agent. B consolidates every job under one maximally privileged shared account.

prompt: A fintech runs a remote MCP server in front of its internal payments API. The server takes whatever OAuth access token the MCP client presents and forwards it unchanged to the payments API, without checking whom the token was issued for. A security review flags this design. Which change addresses the finding?

options.text: Have the MCP server accept only tokens issued for itself, and obtain a separate token for the payments API scoped to the calls the server makes
options.explanation: Correct: audience validation plus a distinct downstream token removes token passthrough, which the MCP authorisation guidance explicitly forbids.

options.text: Keep forwarding the client's token, but require TLS on the connection between the MCP server and the payments API so the token cannot be intercepted
options.explanation: Transport encryption protects the token in transit but leaves the server accepting and relaying tokens that were never meant for it.

options.text: Keep forwarding the client's token, but shorten its lifetime to a few minutes so that a token leaked through the MCP server is useful for less time
options.explanation: Short lifetimes reduce exposure but do not fix the missing audience check or the confused-deputy risk of passing tokens through.

options.text: Let the model pass a payments-API token in each tool call's arguments, so the server no longer needs to handle the client's OAuth token at all
options.explanation: Putting credentials in model-generated arguments exposes them to the model and to injection, which is worse than the original design.

explanation: Correct: A. The MCP authorisation specification requires servers to validate that access tokens were issued for them (audience validation) and explicitly forbids token passthrough; when the server calls an upstream API it must use a separate token obtained for that API, scoped to what the server does. B and C harden the token without fixing the audience problem or the confused-deputy risk. D moves the credential into the model's context, creating a new exposure.

prompt: A university's student-support agent reads module enrolments and grades from the student-records API. It uses one API key, created years ago, that has read and write access to every module, never expires, and is stored in a config file in the code repository. The agent's tools only ever read data. Which change most reduces the risk?

options.text: Replace the key with short-lived tokens issued at run time, scoped to the read operations the tools use and refreshed automatically
options.explanation: Correct: narrow read-only scope and short expiry shrink both what a leaked credential can do and how long it works.

options.text: Keep the existing key but move it out of the repository into an environment variable on the server, so that it no longer appears in version control
options.explanation: Removing it from the repository helps, but the credential is still long-lived and still grants write access to every module.

options.text: Keep the existing key and add a system-prompt rule that the agent must never call any write endpoint of the student-records API
options.explanation: A prompt rule is not an access control; injection or a model error can still reach endpoints the credential allows.

options.text: Rotate the same broad key once a year and raise an alert whenever it is used outside normal office hours, so that misuse is spotted quickly
options.explanation: Annual rotation and alerting detect some misuse but leave a year-long, over-privileged credential in place.

explanation: Correct: A. The key's risk comes from three properties: it is over-scoped (write access the agent never needs), long-lived (no expiry) and poorly stored. Short-lived, automatically refreshed tokens scoped to read-only operations address scope and lifetime at the enforcing layer, and issuing them at run time removes the stored secret. B fixes only storage. C relies on the prompt for authorisation. D adds detection but leaves the over-privileged long-lived key in use.

prompt: A B2B retailer's account agent has a `list_orders` tool that returns every order for a customer as full JSON. For large trade customers this runs to thousands of orders and tens of thousands of tokens, results are sometimes truncated, and the agent misses recent orders. How should the tool be redesigned?

options.text: Raise the maximum tool-output token limit so that the complete order list for even the largest trade customer fits into the context in one response
options.explanation: This keeps flooding the context with mostly irrelevant rows, raising cost and latency and diluting the model's attention.

options.text: Pass the full order list through a second model call that summarises it before returning, so that the agent receives a compact overview instead
options.explanation: A summary adds latency and cost and can drop the specific orders the agent needs, with no way to ask for them.

options.text: Load each customer's complete order history into the system prompt at the start of the session, so that the agent does not need to call the tool
options.explanation: This moves the same oversized payload into every request and goes stale as new orders arrive during the session.

options.text: Add date and status filters, paginate with a modest default page size and concise fields, and return a total count with how to fetch the next page
options.explanation: Correct: filtering, pagination and concise defaults keep results small and relevant, and tell the model how to get more.

explanation: Correct: D. Anthropic's guidance on writing tools for agents recommends returning high-signal results: support filtering and pagination, choose sensible defaults, return concise fields unless detail is requested, and when results are truncated tell the model how to retrieve more. A only enlarges the problem. B adds a lossy, slow step. C moves the oversized, changing data into the prompt on every request.

prompt: A city council's permit-booking agent calls a `book_inspection` tool. When the date is in the wrong format or the slot is already taken, the tool returns only `Error 400`. The agent then either repeats the identical call or tells the resident the system is down. What is the best fix?

options.text: Return a tool error saying what was wrong and how to fix it, such as the expected date format or the nearest free slots
options.explanation: Correct: specific, actionable error content lets the model correct its arguments or offer alternatives instead of guessing.

options.text: Wrap the tool in a retry loop that resends the identical request up to five times before reporting a failure back to the model
options.explanation: Resending the same malformed or conflicting request cannot succeed; it only adds latency and load.

options.text: Suppress the error and return an empty successful result, so that the conversation carries on smoothly without alarming the resident
options.explanation: Hiding the failure leads the model to believe the booking worked or to invent an outcome.

options.text: Return the full stack trace and the internal service logs with each error, so that the model has as much diagnostic detail as possible
options.explanation: Raw internals are noisy, can leak sensitive details, and still do not tell the model what valid input looks like.

explanation: Correct: A. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends error responses that clearly communicate what went wrong and how to correct it, rather than opaque codes or tracebacks, and tool results can be flagged as errors so the model knows the call failed. B retries a request that cannot succeed. C hides the failure and invites fabrication. D floods the model with internals that do not help it fix the input and may expose sensitive data.

prompt: An insurer's RAG assistant indexes 40 policy wordings, chunked by section. Many chunks read like "The excess for this cover is 250 pounds" with no mention of which product they belong to, so questions about home insurance often retrieve the travel or motor policy's chunk. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: At indexing time, prepend to each chunk a short header naming its policy, product, and section, and then embed and index that combined text
options.explanation: Correct: adding situating context to each chunk before indexing makes otherwise identical chunks distinguishable to both retrievers.

options.text: Split the sections into single-sentence chunks so that each embedding captures one precise fact and matches the user's question more closely
options.explanation: Smaller chunks strip away even more context, making chunks from different products harder to tell apart.

options.text: Raise the number of retrieved chunks from five to thirty so that the chunk from the correct product is likely to be somewhere in the results
options.explanation: More results add noise and cost, and the model still cannot tell which of the look-alike chunks belongs to which product.

options.text: Add an instruction telling the model to disregard any retrieved chunk that does not explicitly mention the product the user is asking about
options.explanation: The relevant chunks themselves lack the product name, so this instruction would discard the right answer too.

explanation: Correct: A. The chunks lose the context that distinguishes them once they are cut from their document. Anthropic's contextual retrieval approach prepends chunk-specific context, such as the document and section it comes from, before embedding and before building the keyword index, which sharply reduces retrieval failures. B removes more context. C widens recall without making chunks distinguishable. D filters on a signal the correct chunks do not contain.

prompt: An HR-advice SaaS indexes employment-law guidance for twelve countries, including superseded versions kept for reference. A user in Germany asking about current notice periods often receives semantically similar guidance for Austria or a version that was replaced last year. The user's country is known from their profile. Which retrieval change fits best?

options.text: Append the phrase "for Germany, current rules" to every query before embedding it, so that the query vector leans towards German and up-to-date content
options.explanation: Query wording nudges similarity but cannot reliably exclude near-identical guidance for another country or an old version.

options.text: Train a separate embedding model for each country so that German guidance is embedded in its own vector space and separated from the others
options.explanation: Per-country embedding models are costly to build and maintain, and they still do nothing to exclude superseded versions.

options.text: Store country and effective dates as metadata on each chunk, and filter retrieval on the user's country and on currently effective guidance
options.explanation: Correct: hard metadata filters exclude the wrong jurisdiction and superseded versions before similarity ranking happens.

options.text: Increase the overlap between neighbouring chunks so that each chunk carries more of the surrounding text that names the country and version
options.explanation: Overlap helps with split sentences but does not stop similar content from other countries or old versions outranking the right chunk.

explanation: Correct: C. The query has known structured attributes (country, and the need for current rules) that semantic similarity alone cannot enforce. Storing jurisdiction and effective dates as chunk metadata and filtering on them restricts the candidate set before ranking. A only nudges the vector. B is expensive and ignores versioning. D addresses boundary splits, not jurisdiction or currency.

prompt: A media group switched its RAG pipeline to a new embedding model with better multilingual support. New articles and all incoming queries are now embedded with the new model, but the existing archive was left with vectors from the old model. Retrieval of archive content has become close to random. What should the team do?

options.text: Normalise all vectors in the index to unit length so that similarity scores from the old and new embedding models become directly comparable
options.explanation: Normalisation fixes scale, not meaning; vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces whatever their length.

options.text: Keep the archive vectors and embed each query with the old model as well, merging both result lists into one ranking for the user
options.explanation: This doubles the work and merges scores from incomparable spaces, while keeping the weaker model in service indefinitely.

options.text: Re-embed the whole archive with the new model into a new index, check it on a retrieval test set, and only then switch queries over to it
options.explanation: Correct: queries and documents must be embedded with the same model, so a model change requires a full re-index.

options.text: Leave the archive vectors as they are and add a re-ranking step, which will reorder the results and correct for the mismatch between models
options.explanation: A re-ranker can only reorder the candidates it receives, and the mismatched first stage is not surfacing the right ones.

explanation: Correct: C. Embeddings from different models occupy different vector spaces, so a query vector from the new model cannot be meaningfully compared with document vectors from the old one. Changing embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus, ideally into a parallel index that is validated before cut-over. A changes vector length, not the space. B merges incomparable scores and keeps both models. D cannot recover candidates the first stage never retrieves.

prompt: A freight forwarder's analysts ask questions such as "how many shipments to Rotterdam arrived late last quarter, by carrier?". The team converted each row of the shipments table into a text chunk, embedded it, and lets the assistant retrieve the top 20 chunks. The counts it reports are consistently wrong. What should the architect do?

options.text: Give the agent a parameterised query tool over the shipments database for filters and aggregates, keeping embeddings for documents
options.explanation: Correct: counts and group-bys over structured rows are database queries, which return exact results that similarity search cannot.

options.text: Use larger chunks that each hold a few hundred shipment rows, so that more of the relevant shipments are retrieved within the top 20 results
options.explanation: Bigger chunks still return only a similarity-ranked sample, so totals remain incomplete and unreliable.

options.text: Raise the number of retrieved chunks until it exceeds the number of shipments in a typical quarter, so that every matching row reaches the model
options.explanation: This floods the context with rows and still relies on the model to count accurately across thousands of items.

options.text: Switch to the largest available model so that it reasons more carefully about the retrieved rows and produces more accurate totals
options.explanation: The model is counting an incomplete sample; a stronger model cannot recover rows that retrieval never returned.

explanation: Correct: A. Aggregation questions over a structured table need exact filtering and grouping, which a database query does natively. Vector retrieval returns a similarity-ranked sample of rows, so any count built from it is incomplete. B and C keep the wrong mechanism and only change the sample size. D blames the model for missing data that retrieval never supplied.

prompt: A platform team's Claude Code agents run in sandboxed CI containers and need to check deployment status and roll back releases. The company's mature, well-documented deployment CLI is already installed in those containers, and only this team's agents need it. An engineer proposes building an MCP server that wraps all 40 CLI commands. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Have the agents run the existing CLI via their shell tool, allow-listing the needed subcommands, with sandbox-scoped credentials
options.explanation: Correct: for one team's agents that already have a shell, a mature CLI is a direct, low-cost interface once its permissions are constrained.

options.text: Build the MCP server with one tool per CLI command, so that all 40 operations become discoverable to the agents through their tool definitions
options.explanation: A one-to-one wrapper adds a service to maintain and 40 tool definitions to the context, for a single consumer that can already run the CLI.

options.text: Paste the CLI's complete reference manual into every session's system prompt, so that the agents know the syntax of every command before they start
options.explanation: Loading the whole manual on every run wastes context; the agent can read help output or short project notes when it needs them.

options.text: Stand up a separate deployment agent that the coding agents contact through an agent-to-agent protocol whenever they need status or a rollback
options.explanation: Agent-to-agent suits independently owned agents; here one team owns everything and a tool call suffices.

explanation: Correct: A. When agents already run in a sandbox with a shell and a mature CLI exists, letting them use it directly is often the simplest integration, provided permissions restrict which subcommands run and credentials are scoped to the sandbox. MCP earns its cost when an integration is shared across many clients. B builds a wrapper for one consumer and adds tool bloat. C spends context on a whole manual every run. D introduces agent-to-agent coordination where there is no separate owner.

prompt: A travel agency's booking agent calls a partner airline's API, which returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header during peaks. The tool currently retries immediately in a tight loop, the model sometimes re-issues the call as well, and the team has found duplicate bookings after busy periods. Which design addresses this?

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to wait a few seconds before re-issuing any tool call that has failed with a rate-limit error
options.explanation: The model cannot reliably pause or coordinate timing, and the tool's own tight retry loop would continue regardless.

options.text: In the tool layer, honour Retry-After with capped, jittered backoff, use idempotency keys on bookings, and report clearly when retries run out
options.explanation: Correct: backoff in code respects the limit, idempotency keys make repeated bookings safe, and a clear result stops the model looping.

options.text: Keep retrying immediately but issue several identical requests in parallel, so that at least one of them is likely to get through before the limit resets
options.explanation: Parallel retries amplify the overload, worsen throttling and multiply the chance of duplicate bookings.

options.text: Ask the airline for a higher rate limit and remove all retry logic, so that any failure goes straight back to the customer to try again later
options.explanation: A higher limit may help capacity but peaks will still throttle, and removing retries without idempotency still leaves duplicates possible.

explanation: Correct: B. Rate-limit handling belongs in deterministic code: respect Retry-After, back off exponentially with jitter up to a cap, make non-idempotent operations such as bookings safe to repeat with idempotency keys, and give the model a clear result when the call cannot complete so it does not retry on its own. A leaves timing to the model. C makes the overload worse. D treats capacity as the only issue and ignores duplicate writes.

prompt: An investment bank's research system has an orchestrator agent that delegates to three subagents, each of which calls MCP servers running on different hosts. Every component writes logs with its own request IDs. During incidents, engineers spend hours matching timestamps to reconstruct what happened in a single session. Which change fixes this most directly?

options.text: Synchronise every host's clock precisely, so that timestamps across components line up and events can be correlated by time with confidence
options.explanation: Accurate clocks help ordering but cannot tell which of many concurrent sessions an event belonged to.

options.text: Have each subagent write a short natural-language summary of its work to a shared log when it finishes, for engineers to read during incidents
options.explanation: Self-reported summaries omit failing steps and timing, and they are not linked to the underlying tool and server calls.

options.text: Create a trace ID at the start of each session, propagate it through every subagent, tool and MCP call, and record each step as a span
options.explanation: Correct: one propagated trace context ties every step across hosts into a single tree that can be queried directly.

options.text: Ship all component logs to one central store with full-text search, so that engineers can search on the user's ID across every system
options.explanation: Centralising helps, but a user ID spans many sessions and does not link parent and child steps within one session.

explanation: Correct: C. Distributed tracing gives each session one trace ID that is propagated across process and host boundaries, typically via a standard trace context such as OpenTelemetry, and records each orchestrator step, subagent run, tool call and MCP request as a span with a parent link. Engineers can then open one trace and see the whole tree. A and D improve log handling but cannot reliably separate concurrent sessions or show causality. B relies on agents reporting their own failures.

prompt: An online grocer's product-question assistant has an agreed accuracy target of 88% and a p95 latency budget of 2.5 seconds. On the same test set (where differences under one point are within noise) the team measured: config 1, top-5 retrieval: 86%, 1.3 s. Config 2, top-10: 90%, 1.6 s. Config 3, top-10 with extended thinking: 91%, 3.8 s. Config 4, top-20: 90.5%, 2.2 s. Which decision is best justified?

options.text: Choose config 3, because it has the highest measured accuracy, and ask stakeholders to relax the latency budget so the extra quality can be delivered
options.explanation: Its one-point gain is at the edge of noise and it breaches the agreed latency budget by a wide margin.

options.text: Choose config 1, because it is the fastest and cheapest option, and the two-point shortfall against the accuracy target is small enough to accept
options.explanation: It misses the agreed accuracy target, so it fails a stated requirement rather than trading within the targets.

options.text: Choose config 2, which clears the accuracy target with a margin while staying inside the budget, and record why configs 3 and 4 were both rejected
options.explanation: Correct: it meets both agreed targets, and the alternatives either break the budget or add latency and tokens for a within-noise gain.

options.text: Choose config 4, because it is the most accurate option that still fits within the latency budget, and so it maximises quality under the constraint
options.explanation: Its half-point edge over config 2 is within noise, while it costs more latency headroom and more input tokens per request.

explanation: Correct: C. A justified configuration decision meets the agreed targets and does not pay for differences the evaluation cannot distinguish. Config 2 clears 88% with margin at 1.6 s. A breaks the latency budget for a gain within noise. B fails the accuracy target. D treats a half-point, within-noise difference as real while spending more latency headroom and tokens. Recording the rejected options and the reasons makes the trade-off reviewable if targets change.

prompt: A consultancy's internal agent is connected to nine MCP servers exposing about 250 tools. The tool definitions take up a large share of the context on every request, and tool-selection mistakes are rising. Most requests use three or four tools, and a handful of tools are used in almost every session. Which TWO measures best address this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Merge all 250 tools into one generic `call_tool` tool that takes a tool name and a free-form arguments object
options.explanation: This hides every tool's purpose and parameters from the model, making correct selection and argument construction harder.

options.text: Enable tool search so that most tool definitions are deferred and loaded only when the model searches for them
options.explanation: Correct: deferred loading keeps rarely used definitions out of context until a request actually needs them.

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window so that all 250 definitions fit comfortably alongside the conversation
options.explanation: More room does not reduce the token cost or the selection confusion caused by hundreds of similar tools.

options.text: Shorten every tool description to a single line so that each definition uses as few tokens as possible
options.explanation: Terse descriptions save tokens but make tools harder to tell apart, which worsens selection accuracy.

options.text: Keep the handful of tools used in almost every session loaded up front rather than deferring them
options.explanation: Correct: always-needed tools should stay loaded so common requests do not pay an extra search step.

explanation: Correct: B and E. Anthropic's tool search lets definitions be marked for deferred loading so the model discovers them on demand, which cuts context use and helps selection when there are many tools; the docs recommend leaving the most frequently used tools non-deferred so common requests stay fast. A destroys the information the model needs to choose. C pays for the same bloat with more context. D trades selection accuracy for tokens.

prompt: A customer-service SaaS runs one Claude-based agent for 300 business tenants, each with its own knowledge base and prompt configuration. Last month one tenant's answer quality degraded for two weeks before the tenant complained; platform-wide dashboards showed nothing unusual. Which TWO monitoring strategies would have caught this sooner? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store every full prompt, response and retrieved document for every tenant so that any session can be replayed later
options.explanation: Capturing everything is costly at scale and does not by itself raise an alert when one tenant degrades.

options.text: Track platform-wide average latency, token spend and error rate on a daily dashboard reviewed by the operations team
options.explanation: Platform averages are exactly what hid the problem; one tenant out of 300 barely moves them.

options.text: Have an engineer read ten randomly chosen conversations from across the platform each week and note any problems
options.explanation: Ten random conversations a week will rarely include the affected tenant and gives no trend over time.

options.text: Tag every trace and metric with tenant ID and prompt or knowledge-base version so that quality can be sliced per tenant
options.explanation: Correct: per-tenant and per-version dimensions let a regression confined to one tenant show up instead of averaging away.

options.text: Score a sample of each tenant's production conversations with an automated evaluator and alert on per-tenant drops
options.explanation: Correct: continuous sampled quality scoring detects degradation that latency and error metrics never see.

explanation: Correct: D and E. At multi-tenant scale a local regression disappears in global averages, so traces and metrics need tenant and configuration-version dimensions, and quality itself has to be measured continuously, for example by scoring a sample of each tenant's traffic with an automated evaluator and alerting on drops. A is expensive and passive. B is the averaged view that missed the problem. C samples too little to find a single tenant's issue.

prompt: A chemicals manufacturer is designing a RAG pipeline over safety procedures. Each procedure has numbered steps and tables of exposure limits. Operators usually ask about one specific step, but answers are only safe if the surrounding steps and limits are included. Which TWO design choices fit best? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use fixed 100-token chunks with no overlap to maximise precision when matching a specific step
options.explanation: Fixed tiny chunks split steps and tables and hand the model fragments without their safety context.

options.text: Embed each complete procedure manual as a single vector so that no context is ever separated from its steps
options.explanation: One vector per long manual blurs many topics together, so matching on a specific step becomes unreliable.

options.text: Index step-level chunks for matching, but pass the whole enclosing procedure to the model when a step matches
options.explanation: Correct: small units match precisely while the returned parent section keeps adjacent steps and limits together.

options.text: Strip the tables out before indexing, because embedding models handle tabular content poorly
options.explanation: Removing the exposure-limit tables throws away information the answers must include.

options.text: Retrieve a wider candidate set, then re-rank it and keep only the most relevant few for the model
options.explanation: Correct: a re-ranking stage improves which candidates reach the model without shrinking first-stage recall.

explanation: Correct: C and E. Matching on small units while returning the larger parent section (small-to-big retrieval) gives precise hits without losing the surrounding steps and limits that safety answers depend on, and retrieving broadly then re-ranking improves precision of what reaches the model. A fragments procedures. B makes step-level matching unreliable. D deletes the tables operators need.

prompt: An architect is deciding whether a new agent should discover tools and reference material on demand or load everything into context up front. Which TWO characteristics most strongly favour loading everything up front? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The agent spans many business domains and has a few hundred tools, each used by only a small share of requests
options.explanation: A large, rarely used catalogue is the classic case for on-demand discovery, not for loading everything.

options.text: The reference material is large and parts of it change every hour as upstream systems publish updates
options.explanation: Large, fast-changing material bloats every request and keeps invalidating any cached prefix, which favours fetching on demand.

options.text: The toolset is small and stable, nearly every request uses most of it, and the fixed prefix can be prompt-cached
options.explanation: Correct: when almost everything is needed every time and the prefix is cacheable, up-front loading is cheap and avoids discovery steps.

options.text: A strict latency budget would be breached by an extra discovery round-trip, and the full context fits easily
options.explanation: Correct: if everything fits and latency is tight, avoiding a search or fetch turn is worth the extra tokens.

options.text: Requests vary widely and each one needs a different small subset of the available tools and documents
options.explanation: Varied requests that each touch a small subset are what progressive discovery is designed for.

explanation: Correct: C and D. Monolithic context wins when the material is small, stable and needed on almost every request, so prompt caching makes the repeated prefix cheap, and when an added discovery round-trip would break a latency budget that the full context comfortably fits within. A and E describe large or varied needs that progressive discovery serves better. B describes content that is too large and volatile to load and cache on every request.

prompt: A steering group asks whether a new policy-lookup assistant is "good enough to launch". The team has enthusiastic quotes from pilot users but no measurements. What should the architect put in place first?

options.text: A longer pilot with more users, so there are more quotes and anecdotes to present to the steering group
A dashboard of token spend and latency, which are the metrics the platform already emits
Run the offline evaluation suite the platform team already uses for its other assistants
Defined metrics for accuracy, latency, cost and safety, with launch thresholds agreed with the business

explanation: Correct: D. "Good enough" has to be defined before it can be measured: agree the metrics and the thresholds that count as ready, then measure against them. A collects more anecdotes. B measures what is easy rather than what matters, and leaves out accuracy and safety. C borrows another system's metrics before this one's targets have been defined.

prompt: A team is assembling an evaluation dataset for a travel-booking assistant before launch. Which composition gives the most trustworthy signal?

options.text: Two hundred synthetic conversations generated by the assistant's own model and graded automatically by that same model
The twenty conversations from the sales demo deck, since those are the ones stakeholders will try first
Real anonymised conversations plus hard, adversarial and edge cases, each with a reference answer
Whatever pilot users typed in the first week, without reference answers, graded by thumbs-up counts

explanation: Correct: C. A trustworthy evaluation set reflects real traffic, includes the hard and adversarial cases that break systems, and has reference answers and rubrics so grading is consistent. A measures the model against itself on data it generated. B is a tiny, flattering sample. D has no ground truth, so a confident wrong answer and a right one score the same.

prompt: A marketing-copy assistant must be checked for tone and brand alignment across thousands of outputs a week. Reviewing every output by hand is not feasible. Which evaluation method fits?

options.text: A model-as-judge grader with a written rubric, calibrated against a human-labelled sample
Exact string matching of each output against a bank of approved reference copy for the same product
A weekly review of ten randomly chosen outputs by the brand team, with no other automated checks
Measuring the average length of outputs, since on-brand copy tends to fall within a consistent length range

explanation: Correct: A. Tone and brand are subjective qualities that string matching cannot measure; a model grader working from a rubric scales to thousands of outputs, provided it is calibrated against human judgements and monitored for drift. B fails on any valid rewording. C covers a fraction of a percent of output and misses systematic problems. D measures a proxy with no real relation to tone.

prompt: A revised prompt beats the current production prompt by five points on the offline evaluation suite. The team wants confidence before replacing it for all users. What is the right next step?

options.text: Replace the production prompt immediately, because the offline suite is the agreed quality gate
Ask the pilot users which of the two prompts they prefer in a short survey before deciding
Re-run the offline suite several more times until the gap is statistically convincing, then deploy
Run an A/B test on a fraction of live traffic and compare the agreed metrics before full rollout

explanation: Correct: D. Offline gains do not always hold on live traffic; an A/B test on real requests with pre-agreed metrics is how the gain is confirmed, with a small blast radius if it does not hold. A skips the live check. C only tightens an offline estimate. B measures preference on a tiny sample rather than the agreed metrics on real traffic.

prompt: A finance director asks for a 40% cut in a solution's inference bill. The team's first proposal is to switch every workload to the smallest model. What should the architect do before agreeing?

options.text: Agree, since the cost target is a business decision and the smallest model is the fastest way to it
Refuse, since model downgrades always lower quality and the proposal should not be entertained
Profile the spend, then test cheaper options per workload against the evaluation suite
Switch only the most expensive workload to the smallest model and wait to see whether anyone complains

explanation: Correct: C. Cost optimisation starts by measuring where tokens go, then applies the cheapest change that holds quality, verified by evaluation; the smallest model may be right for some workloads and wrong for others. A and D change production without measuring quality. B rejects a reasonable goal instead of finding the safe route to it.

prompt: A team is moving production traffic to a newly released model version. Spot checks look fine. Which rollout practice best protects production quality?

options.text: Switch all traffic at once during a quiet period so that any problems surface quickly and at low volume
Run the evaluation suite on the new version, then roll out gradually with monitoring and a rollback path
Keep the old version indefinitely, since a system that is working should not be changed
Switch the staging environment only and leave production on the old version until users request the new one

explanation: Correct: B. A model change is a change to system behaviour: evaluate it against the suite, then expose it gradually with monitoring and rollback. A makes the whole user base the test. C ignores deprecation and improvement. D never completes the migration and gains no evidence about production behaviour.

prompt: An architect wants early warning of quality degradation in a production RAG assistant, before users start complaining. Which signal is the most useful leading indicator?

options.text: The number of support tickets that mention the assistant, reviewed by the team at the end of each month
Total monthly token spend compared with the budget that was approved for the assistant
The uptime percentage of the retrieval service and the vector database behind it
Retrieval quality on sampled live queries, such as relevance scores and unsupported answers

explanation: Correct: D. In a RAG system quality usually breaks at retrieval first, so monitoring retrieval relevance and unsupported answers on a live sample shows degradation before it reaches the user. A is a lagging indicator by definition. B tracks cost, not quality. C says the service is up, not that it returns the right chunks.

prompt: A summarisation feature using a small, fast model produces accurate summaries of short emails but consistently drops key points from 50-page reports, even with a well-structured prompt. Which system issue is this?

options.text: A hallucination, since the summaries contain content that the source reports do not actually contain
A prompt failure, since the instructions about completeness are not being followed
A retrieval failure, since the wrong parts of the long reports are being fetched
A model mismatch: the model copes with the short task but not the long, demanding one

explanation: Correct: D. The same prompt works on easy inputs and fails on hard ones, which points to the model's capability on long, dense documents rather than the prompt; the fix is a more capable model or decomposition. A describes invented content, but the problem here is omission. B is unlikely when the identical prompt succeeds on short inputs. C does not apply: there is no retrieval step.

prompt: A parcel-tracking assistant invents a plausible tracking number when the lookup tool returns no result, instead of telling the customer that nothing was found. What is the issue and the most direct fix?

options.text: A hallucination; define the empty-result behaviour and validate numbers against the tool output
A model mismatch; move to a larger model, which will know the correct tracking numbers for the parcels in question
A retrieval failure; add more parcels to the index so that the lookup tool returns a result more often
A latency issue; the tool is timing out and the model fills the gap, so increase the tool's timeout

explanation: Correct: A. Fabricating a value to fill a gap is a hallucination; the fix is to specify the empty-result behaviour in the prompt and to check output values against what the tool actually returned. B is wrong because no model knows tracking numbers it was not given. C misreads a correct empty result as a failure. D invents a cause the scenario does not describe.

prompt: An assistant told to "answer in two sentences" keeps producing long answers. Inspection of the system prompt finds a later section that says "explain your reasoning fully". Which issue is this?

options.text: A model mismatch, since a more capable model would reconcile the two instructions sensibly
A prompt failure from conflicting instructions: remove the contradiction and state the intent once
A hallucination, since the model is generating content that the user did not ask it to produce
A context-window problem, since the prompt is too long for the model to take all of it into account at once

explanation: Correct: B. Two instructions that cannot both be satisfied are a prompt defect; the model is following one of them. A asks a model to resolve an ambiguity the author should remove. C is wrong because the content is relevant, just too long. D is not indicated by anything in the scenario.

prompt: A document-analysis pipeline's p95 latency is 9 seconds. Tracing shows three sequential model calls of about 2.5 seconds each plus a 1.5-second retrieval step, and the second and third calls do not depend on each other. Which optimisation gives the largest latency reduction without changing quality?

options.text: Run the second and third calls in parallel, cutting about 2.5 seconds from the critical path
Enable prompt caching on all three calls, which will make each of them return almost instantly
Move all three calls to the smallest model to roughly halve the time taken by each one
Remove the retrieval step and rely on the model's own knowledge of the documents instead

explanation: Correct: A. The trace shows two independent calls run in sequence; parallelising them removes a whole call from the critical path with no change to outputs. B reduces time-to-first-token on cached prefixes but does not eliminate generation time. C changes quality, which the question rules out. D removes grounding and will change answers.

prompt: A nightly job classifies 300,000 documents. Results are needed by the next morning and nobody waits on an individual document. Which change most reduces cost without changing the model or the prompt?

options.text: Run the requests through the synchronous API with higher concurrency so the job finishes sooner
Shorten every document to its first paragraph before classification to cut the input tokens
Retry each request several times and keep the cheapest response that comes back from the model
Submit the documents through the batch API, trading latency the job does not need for a lower price

explanation: Correct: D. Batch processing is the designed trade: asynchronous completion within a window in exchange for a lower price, which fits a nightly job with no interactive user. A finishes faster but does not cost less. B changes the inputs and therefore the results. C makes no sense: pricing is per token, and retries add cost.

prompt: A team is defining metrics for an internal HR assistant. Which set covers the dimensions a complete evaluation plan should address?

options.text: Accuracy, since an assistant that gives correct answers is a good assistant
Accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security, each with a target and a way to measure it
Latency and cost, because those are the two metrics the platform reports automatically
User satisfaction score, because the users of the assistant are the final judges

explanation: Correct: B. An evaluation plan covers accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security together, each with a measurable target; optimising one in isolation hides regressions in the others. A ignores whether the system is affordable, fast enough or safe. C ignores whether it is right. D is useful but lagging, subjective and silent on safety and cost.
