prompt: A team is designing the pre-production evaluation framework for an assistant that will operate in a regulated industry. Which TWO components are most important to include? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A demo script that shows the assistant's best answers to executives and the regulator's liaison
A held-out test set with reference answers that the prompt was never tuned against
Adversarial cases that probe prompt injection, policy-violating requests and safety limits, graded by domain experts
A single aggregate quality score so that the results are simple to communicate to leadership
Evaluation run only on the final day before launch so that the results reflect the shipped version

explanation: Correct: B and C. A regulated setting needs a clean held-out set with reference answers (so scores are not inflated by tuning) and adversarial cases, graded by people who know the domain, showing that the boundaries hold under attack. A is marketing, not evaluation. D hides the per-category failures a regulator will ask about. E leaves no time to act on the findings.

prompt: A production assistant's answer quality has degraded gradually over two weeks. Latency, model version and prompts are unchanged. Which TWO data sources are most useful for finding the cause? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Traces of failing sessions showing which chunks were retrieved and which tools were called
The total number of requests per day over the two weeks, broken down by hour and by channel
The team's on-call roster showing who was responsible for the system on each of the days
The model provider's public status page and its incident history for the two-week period
The mix of live inputs over the two weeks, checked for new query types, formats or languages

explanation: Correct: A and E. With model, prompt and latency ruled out, what changed is what flows through the system: session traces show what the model was given in the failing cases, and the input mix shows whether the traffic has drifted away from what the system was designed and evaluated for. B and C are unlikely to explain a gradual quality change. D matters for outages, not gradual degradation with an unchanged model.

prompt: A team wants to reduce token usage on a long-running support conversation without harming answer quality. Which TWO techniques apply? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Delete the system prompt after the first turn, since the model will remember it for the session
Summarise or compact older turns past a length threshold, keeping the facts the assistant still needs
Send the full conversation twice per turn to be sure that nothing important is lost
Replace every tool result with the word "done" the moment it is returned to save tokens
Prune large tool results from earlier turns once used, leaving a short note of what was found

explanation: Correct: B and E. Context management for long sessions means compacting history and clearing bulky tool outputs once they have served their purpose, while preserving the information still needed. A breaks the assistant: each request is stateless and the system prompt must be sent every time. C doubles cost. D destroys information before it is used.

prompt: A freight forwarder uses Claude to extract the HS code, declared value, currency and country of origin from customs invoices into a fixed JSON schema. The team has 400 invoices whose correct field values were already keyed in by brokers. Which grading method fits this evaluation best?

options.text: Code-based grading that parses each output and compares every field with the broker-keyed values
options.explanation: Right: the expected values are known and exact, so a deterministic comparison is fast, cheap, reproducible and unbiased.

options.text: A model-graded rubric asking a second model to rate each extraction for overall accuracy on a 1-to-5 scale
options.explanation: A judge model adds cost and variance where an exact comparison against known values is already possible.

options.text: Human review of every extraction by customs specialists, who mark each invoice as acceptable or not acceptable
options.explanation: Slow and expensive for a task with known correct answers; humans are better spent on ambiguous or subjective outputs.

options.text: Semantic similarity between the JSON output and the broker record, scored by an embedding model with a pass threshold
options.explanation: Similarity scores blur exact values; a wrong HS code or currency can still look very similar to the right one.

explanation: Correct: A. When the task has an objectively correct answer that is already known, code-based grading (parse the JSON, compare each field exactly) is the fastest, most reliable and most scalable method, and it reports accuracy per field. B introduces a judge's variance and cost for no gain. C reserves expensive expert time for a check a script can do. D treats near-misses such as a wrong digit in an HS code as nearly correct.

prompt: A news publisher compares two headline-writing prompts with a pairwise model judge: the judge sees headline 1 and headline 2 and names the better one. Prompt X's headline is always shown first. X wins 71% of comparisons, but editors reviewing a sample see little difference. What should the architect change first?

options.text: Switch the judge to a larger model, since a stronger model will be less swayed by superficial features of the pair
options.explanation: Larger judges still show position bias; the fixed ordering confound remains and must be removed in the test design.

options.text: Ask the judge for a numeric score per headline instead of a preference, then average the scores per prompt variant
options.explanation: Can help, but it leaves the identified confound untested; the cheaper first step is to check whether order alone drives the result.

options.text: Present every pair in both orders, and count a win only when the judge prefers the same headline on both occasions
options.explanation: Right: swapping order exposes and neutralises position bias, and inconsistent verdicts are treated as ties.

options.text: Keep the setup but raise the number of comparisons tenfold so that the 71% figure becomes statistically robust
options.explanation: More samples make a biased estimate more precise, not more correct; the systematic order effect persists.

explanation: Correct: C. Model judges are known to favour a response because of its position, so always placing X first confounds the comparison. Running each pair in both orders and counting only consistent preferences removes the bias and shows how often the judge is merely following order. A assumes size cures the bias. B changes the format without testing the confound. D makes a biased number look more certain.

prompt: An airline's refund agent will act for customers without human review, so a case that works on one attempt and fails on the next is unacceptable. Each of 120 test scenarios has been run once; 92% passed. Repeated runs at the production temperature show variation. Which metric best reflects the reliability the business needs?

options.text: pass@k: the share of scenarios in which at least one of k repeated runs succeeds, reported for several values of k
options.explanation: pass@k rewards getting it right once in k tries, which suits pick-the-best workflows, not unattended actions.

options.text: The single-run pass rate, re-measured after setting temperature to zero so that every run of a scenario is identical
options.explanation: Lower temperature reduces but does not remove variation, and it measures a configuration that differs from production.

options.text: The mean pass rate over k runs per scenario, so that occasional failures average out across the whole suite
options.explanation: An average hides which scenarios are flaky; a 90% mean can come from many scenarios that fail one run in ten.

options.text: The share of scenarios in which all of k repeated runs succeed, tracked alongside a list of the inconsistent ones
options.explanation: Right: requiring every trial to pass (often called pass^k) measures consistency, which is what unattended actions demand.

explanation: Correct: D. For an agent acting unattended, reliability means succeeding every time, so the right metric counts scenarios where all k trials pass and lists the flaky ones for diagnosis. A (pass@k) measures the chance of at least one success and rises with k, the opposite of what is needed. B evaluates a different configuration and still may not be deterministic. C averages away the inconsistency that matters.

prompt: At a SaaS company, five engineers edit the system prompts of a billing assistant. Twice this quarter a small wording change fixed one complaint but broke invoice-dispute handling, which was only noticed by customers. How should the team prevent this?

options.text: Version the prompts and run a regression eval suite on every change, blocking any merges below the per-category thresholds
options.explanation: Right: prompts are code; automated per-category checks in CI catch a regression in dispute handling before release.

options.text: Require a senior engineer to read and approve every prompt diff, checking that the new wording cannot affect other topics
options.explanation: Review helps, but people cannot reliably predict how wording shifts behaviour on other topics; that needs measurement.

options.text: Freeze the system prompt and handle new complaints by adding post-processing rules in application code after generation
options.explanation: Avoids prompt regressions by blocking improvement and accumulating brittle patches; it does not create a safety net.

options.text: Run a monthly evaluation of the production assistant and roll back to the previous prompt if the overall score has dropped
options.explanation: Monthly and aggregate: customers meet the regression first, and an overall score can hide a single broken category.

explanation: Correct: A. Treating prompts like code, with versioning and an automated regression suite that runs on every change and enforces thresholds per category (including invoice disputes), catches unintended side effects before customers see them. B relies on human prediction of model behaviour. C stops iteration instead of protecting it. D detects problems late and can hide a category-specific drop in an aggregate.

prompt: A travel agency's booking agent is evaluated by comparing its tool calls with a recorded reference sequence. Reviewers find that many failed runs actually produced the correct booking by a different valid route, such as checking availability before prices. A few passing runs also issued an unnecessary cancellation. How should the evaluation be redesigned?

options.text: Loosen the matcher so a run passes when at least 80% of its tool calls appear somewhere in the reference sequence
options.explanation: Still ties grading to one path and would continue to pass runs that made a harmful extra cancellation.

options.text: Record several reference sequences per scenario and pass a run when it exactly matches any one of the recorded routes
options.explanation: Valid routes keep multiplying; this stays brittle and still ignores whether forbidden actions were taken.

options.text: Grade the end state of the booking system, and check transcripts explicitly for prohibited actions
options.explanation: Right: outcome grading accepts any valid route, while targeted transcript checks catch harmful steps such as needless cancellations.

options.text: Drop automated grading and have travel consultants read each transcript and judge whether the agent behaved sensibly overall
options.explanation: Human review is useful for calibration, but it does not scale to regression runs and is less consistent than defined checks.

explanation: Correct: C. Agents can reach the right result by many legitimate paths, so grading the outcome (the end state of the booking system) avoids penalising valid variation, while explicit transcript checks catch steps that must never happen, such as an unrequested cancellation. A and B keep grading tied to particular paths and miss harmful actions. D is too slow and inconsistent to be the main regression method.

prompt: A law firm's RAG assistant over case files scores 74% on end-to-end answer correctness, down from 85% after a re-indexing project. Engineers disagree on whether retrieval or generation is at fault. Which evaluation change settles the question fastest?

options.text: Rerun the end-to-end suite with a larger model; if the score recovers, the generation step was at fault
options.explanation: A stronger model can partly compensate for poor retrieval, so the result would not cleanly separate the two stages.

options.text: Measure recall@k on labelled passages and, separately, whether answers are grounded in what was retrieved
options.explanation: Right: stage-level metrics show whether the relevant passages are retrieved and whether the answer stays faithful to them.

options.text: Ask lawyers to rate a sample of answers for overall usefulness so that the team has a richer quality signal
options.explanation: A richer end-to-end rating is still end-to-end; it does not show which stage is causing the drop.

options.text: Add an instruction telling the model to cite its sources, then compare the answer score before and after
options.explanation: Changes the system instead of diagnosing it; any score movement would still mix retrieval and generation effects.

explanation: Correct: B. Retrieval and generation need separate metrics: recall@k on labelled relevant passages shows whether re-indexing broke retrieval, and groundedness (faithfulness to the retrieved context) shows whether the model is using what it was given. A and C remain end-to-end and confound the stages. D is a fix applied before the cause is known, and its effect also mixes both stages.

prompt: A university's student-services assistant runs an A/B test of a new prompt. After two days and about 150 rated conversations per arm, the new prompt has 81% positive ratings against 78% for the current one. The product owner wants to switch everyone over today. What should the architect advise?

options.text: Switch now, since a three-point gain in positive ratings is a meaningful improvement for a student-facing service
options.explanation: With about 150 ratings per arm, a three-point gap is well within the noise; the gain may not be real.

options.text: Switch now but keep the old prompt available, so that it can be restored if complaints rise over the next term
options.explanation: Rollback is useful, but this still decides on a difference the data cannot yet distinguish from chance.

options.text: Estimate the sample size needed to detect a gain of this size, and keep running the test until that size is reached
options.explanation: Right: deciding the required sample in advance and reaching it is what makes the comparison trustworthy.

options.text: Stop the test and rely on the offline evaluation suite, since user ratings are too subjective to guide prompt changes
options.explanation: User ratings are a valid online signal; the problem is sample size, not the kind of metric.

explanation: Correct: C. A three-point difference on roughly 150 ratings per arm has a wide confidence interval and is easily produced by chance or by day-of-week effects, so the team should work out the sample needed to detect a gain of that size and run until it is reached. A and B act on noise. D discards a legitimate online signal instead of collecting enough of it.

prompt: A health insurer tightened the safety instructions of its member assistant after it once gave risky advice about combining medicines. The harmful-response rate on the red-team set fell to near zero. Which measurement should accompany that result before the change is judged a success?

options.text: The false-refusal rate on legitimate but sensitive member questions, such as those about mental-health coverage
options.explanation: Right: over-tightening shows up as refusals of benign questions, which only a benign-sensitive set will reveal.

options.text: The harmful-response rate on a second, larger red-team set, to confirm the near-zero figure is not a sampling fluke
options.explanation: Useful for confidence, but it measures the same side of the trade-off and cannot reveal over-refusal.

options.text: The average length of responses before and after the change, since safer answers tend to be noticeably shorter
options.explanation: Length is a weak proxy; it says nothing direct about whether legitimate questions are now being declined.

options.text: The latency and token cost of the longer system prompt, to confirm the extra instructions are affordable at volume
options.explanation: Worth tracking, but cost is not the main risk created by stricter safety instructions.

explanation: Correct: A. Safety guardrails trade two error types: harmful completions and false refusals. A near-zero harmful rate is only a success if members with legitimate sensitive questions are still being answered, so a benign-but-sensitive set with a false-refusal metric must be measured alongside it. B re-measures the same side. C is an indirect proxy. D tracks a secondary concern.

prompt: A wealth-management firm's research agent reads third-party filings and web pages and can send emails and create tasks. The security team wants each new release to be assessed for prompt-injection resistance in a way that is comparable from release to release. What should the evaluation include?

options.text: A one-off penetration test by an external firm before launch, with its report attached to the release documentation
options.explanation: Valuable, but a one-off test does not give a repeatable measure for each subsequent release.

options.text: A versioned set of injections hidden in documents and tool results, scored by whether forbidden actions occur
options.explanation: Right: a fixed, growing attack suite with an objective success criterion gives a comparable attack-success rate per release.

options.text: A set of direct user requests asking the agent to ignore its instructions, graded on whether the agent politely declines
options.explanation: Covers only direct injection; the main risk here is indirect injection through content the agent reads.

options.text: A model judge that reads each production response and flags any that look as though they were influenced by an injection
options.explanation: Monitoring helps in production, but appearance-based judging is not a controlled, repeatable pre-release test.

explanation: Correct: B. A red-team suite of injection payloads embedded where the agent actually meets untrusted text (filings, pages, tool results), graded on whether a forbidden email or task is actually produced, yields an attack-success rate that can be compared across releases and extended as new attacks appear. A is not repeatable. C ignores indirect injection. D is monitoring, not a controlled evaluation.

prompt: A telecom's chat assistant takes about six seconds to produce a typical answer, and the interface shows a spinner until the full response arrives. Abandonment analysis shows most users leave within the first three seconds. Which change most improves the experience without changing the model?

options.text: Switch to the Batch API so that requests are processed more efficiently and the per-answer cost goes down
options.explanation: Batch processing is asynchronous and suits offline workloads; it would make interactive answers slower, not faster.

options.text: Stream the response so text appears as it is generated, and track time-to-first-token as a separate metric
options.explanation: Right: streaming cuts perceived wait to the time to first token, which is the moment users are abandoning.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` so the model is never cut off, avoiding follow-up questions that add more waiting time
options.explanation: A higher limit does not speed up generation and does nothing for the initial wait that drives abandonment.

options.text: Show a progress bar based on average total latency so that users can see roughly how long the answer will take
options.explanation: A better spinner still makes users wait six seconds for any content to appear.

explanation: Correct: B. Users are abandoning before the answer appears, so the metric that matters is time to first token, not total latency. Streaming the response shows text within a fraction of the total generation time, and tracking TTFT separately shows whether that improvement holds. A suits offline jobs, not live chat. C does not affect speed. D only decorates the wait.

prompt: A city council's permit-guidance assistant has a short system prompt and short user questions, but answers average 700 output tokens: they restate the question, add a preamble and repeat a closing summary. Traces show most latency and cost come from generation. Which change best reduces both while protecting quality?

options.text: Add prompt caching for the system prompt, since cached prompts are cheaper and faster to process on each request
options.explanation: Caching reduces input-processing cost and time, but here the input is small and the output dominates.

options.text: Set `max_tokens` to 250 so that the model physically cannot produce the long answers that drive the cost
options.explanation: A hard cap truncates answers mid-sentence instead of making them concise; it fails users rather than shortening responses.

options.text: Move to a larger model, which tends to follow instructions more closely and so writes shorter, better answers
options.explanation: A larger model is usually slower and costlier per token; verbosity here comes from the output specification.

options.text: Specify a concise format with no restatement or summary, and confirm on the evaluation set that quality holds
options.explanation: Right: removing redundant output cuts the dominant cost and latency, and the eval run guards against losing substance.

explanation: Correct: D. Output tokens drive both latency and cost here, and much of the output is redundant, so tightening the answer specification (no restated question, no preamble, no repeated summary) directly reduces them; rerunning the evaluation confirms quality is preserved. A optimises input, which is already small. B truncates rather than condenses. C typically raises per-token cost and latency.

prompt: A manufacturer's quality team uses Claude to turn inspection reports into a JSON list of defects. About 3% of responses fail to parse, almost all from the longest reports, and each failing response ends partway through an object. What should the engineer check first?

options.text: Whether the prompt's example JSON contains a syntax error that the model is copying into some of its outputs
options.explanation: A copied error would appear across report sizes and at the same place, not as cut-off endings on long inputs.

options.text: The `stop_reason` field of the failing responses, to tell whether those responses hit the `max_tokens` limit
options.explanation: Right: endings cut off mid-object on the longest inputs point to truncation, which the stop reason confirms directly.

options.text: Whether the model is hallucinating defects in long reports, producing malformed entries when it is uncertain
options.explanation: Hallucinated content would usually still be well-formed JSON; it does not explain responses that stop abruptly.

options.text: Whether long reports exceed the context window, causing the model to lose the schema instructions at the top
options.explanation: Exceeding the context window would cause the request to fail, not a well-started response that stops partway.

explanation: Correct: B. Responses that end mid-object, concentrated on the longest inputs, are the signature of output truncation. The API reports `stop_reason: max_tokens` in that case, so checking it confirms the cause; the fix is a higher limit or splitting the output. A would not correlate with input length or end abruptly. C would usually still produce valid JSON. D would produce an error, not a truncated reply.

prompt: A recruitment platform refined its CV-screening prompt through 40 iterations, each time checking the same 60 test CVs and fixing whichever ones failed. The prompt now scores 98% on that set, yet recruiters report that its shortlists on live vacancies are no better than before. What is the most likely explanation and response?

options.text: The model is too small for screening; move to a larger model and repeat the 40-iteration tuning process on the same set
options.explanation: Nothing points to model capacity; repeating the same tuning loop would reproduce the same problem.

options.text: Recruiters are biased against the new system; show them the 98% score and the test cases to build their confidence
options.explanation: Dismisses real field evidence; a gap between test and live results is a signal to investigate, not to persuade.

options.text: The live vacancies differ from the test set; replace the 60 CVs with 60 new ones and continue tuning against those instead
options.explanation: Swapping one small tuning set for another repeats the overfitting unless a separate held-out set is kept.

options.text: The prompt is overfitted to the test set; build a larger held-out set from live vacancies and never use it for tuning
options.explanation: Right: repeated tuning against one small set fits its quirks; only untouched, representative data measures real performance.

explanation: Correct: D. Iterating many times on the same 60 cases and patching each failure fits the prompt to that set's quirks, so its score stops predicting live performance. The remedy is a larger, representative held-out set drawn from live vacancies that is used only for measurement. A assumes a capacity problem with no evidence. B ignores the signal. C repeats the same mistake on new data.

prompt: A logistics company has agreed a service-level objective that 95% of its dispatch assistant's responses complete within four seconds. The assistant performs retrieval, two tool calls and one model call per request. Which TWO monitoring practices best support this objective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Alert whenever any single request exceeds four seconds, so that the on-call engineer sees every slow response immediately
options.explanation: The objective allows 5% of requests to be slower; per-request alerts create noise and alert fatigue.

options.text: Report the daily average response time to the operations director, with a red flag when it rises above four seconds
options.explanation: An average can stay under four seconds while the slowest tail breaches the objective, and daily reporting is too slow.

options.text: Log the full prompt and response of every request so that slow requests can be replayed later during incident reviews
options.explanation: Full payloads help some investigations but do not measure latency or show which step is slow.

options.text: Alert when the p95 latency over a rolling window approaches four seconds, before the objective is actually breached
options.explanation: Right: alerting on the percentile the objective is defined on, with headroom, gives early warning of a breach.

options.text: Record per-step timings for retrieval, each tool call and the model call under one trace ID for every request
options.explanation: Right: step-level spans show which stage is pushing the tail up, turning an alert into a diagnosis.

explanation: Correct: D and E. The objective is defined on the 95th percentile, so alerting on rolling p95 with headroom warns before a breach (D), and per-step spans linked by a trace ID show whether retrieval, a tool or the model is responsible (E). A alerts on requests the objective already allows to be slow. B hides the tail behind an average. C stores content but does not measure or localise latency.

prompt: An insurer uses a model judge to score claim-file summaries with the instruction "rate this summary from 1 to 10 for quality". Analysis shows the judge's scores rise with summary length, and claims handlers often disagree with its rankings. Which TWO changes most improve the judge's reliability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Replace the single score with a rubric of specific criteria, such as omitted facts and unsupported claims, each with defined levels
options.explanation: Right: specific, anchored criteria give the judge something concrete to check instead of rewarding apparent thoroughness.

options.text: Widen the scale from 1-to-10 to 1-to-100 so that the judge can express finer differences between similar summaries
options.explanation: A finer scale adds false precision; it does not address the vague criterion or the length bias.

options.text: Have the same model and prompt that wrote the summaries act as judge, so that it understands the intent behind them
options.explanation: Self-grading invites self-preference and shares the generator's blind spots, weakening the evaluation.

options.text: Score a sample that claims handlers have also graded, and track the judge's agreement with them before trusting its results
options.explanation: Right: calibrating against expert labels shows whether the judge can be trusted and whether rubric changes help.

options.text: Tell the judge to give its score immediately without writing any explanation, which keeps grading fast and avoids rationalisation
options.explanation: Asking for reasoning before the score usually improves judge quality; suppressing it tends to make scores less reliable.

explanation: Correct: A and D. A vague "quality" score lets superficial features such as length drive the result, so a rubric with specific, anchored criteria (A) focuses the judge on what matters, and checking agreement with claims handlers' grades (D) shows whether the judge is trustworthy. B adds false precision. C introduces self-preference. E removes the reasoning step that tends to make judgements more reliable.

prompt: An online retailer wants to A/B test a new product-question prompt on live traffic before replacing the current one. Which TWO design choices are most important for the result to be trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Randomly assign users to each variant and keep each user on the same variant for the duration of the test
options.explanation: Right: random, sticky assignment removes selection bias and stops users seeing both variants within a session.

options.text: Run the new prompt this week and compare its metrics with last week's results from the current prompt
options.explanation: Sequential comparison confounds the prompt with seasonality, promotions and other changes between the weeks.

options.text: Let customers choose to try the new assistant from a banner, so that only willing users are exposed to it
options.explanation: Self-selected users differ systematically from the rest, so any difference cannot be attributed to the prompt.

options.text: Send the new prompt only to the smallest regional storefront so that any harm is limited to a few customers
options.explanation: Limits risk but produces a small, unrepresentative sample whose results may not generalise to other storefronts.

options.text: Fix the primary metric and guardrail metrics, such as escalation rate and cost, before the test starts
options.explanation: Right: pre-registering metrics prevents picking whichever number looks good afterwards and catches harmful side effects.

explanation: Correct: A and E. Random, sticky assignment makes the two groups comparable (A), and fixing the primary and guardrail metrics in advance stops after-the-fact metric shopping while watching for side effects such as more escalations or higher cost (E). B confounds the change with time. C introduces self-selection bias. D trades representativeness for safety and may not generalise.

prompt: An agent can draft supplier emails, update internal records and raise purchase orders up to 40,000 euros. The business wants human oversight without slowing every interaction. Where should the human approval gate go?

options.text: Before every action the agent takes, so that nothing at all happens without a person seeing it first
Nowhere; the agent's spending limit of 40,000 euros is itself a sufficient control
After each purchase order is sent, as part of a weekly review of all the orders the agent raised
Before irreversible or costly actions such as raising a purchase order; drafting and updates run free

explanation: Correct: D. Human-in-the-loop gates belong where the consequence is high and hard to undo; low-risk, reversible actions can flow freely. A defeats the purpose of automation. B treats a spending cap as oversight, which it is not. C reviews after the money has been committed.

prompt: A European retailer's assistant sends complete customer chats, including names and addresses, to a third-party analytics service outside the EU for quality monitoring. The data protection officer objects under GDPR. Which architectural change best answers the objection?

options.text: Add a line to the privacy policy stating that chats may be analysed by a provider outside the EU for quality purposes
Keep sending the full chats but encrypt them in transit and at rest with the analytics provider
Pseudonymise or strip personal data before export, send only what monitoring needs, and use a lawful transfer mechanism
Stop quality monitoring entirely so that no customer data ever leaves the retailer's own systems

explanation: Correct: C. GDPR compliance in the architecture means data minimisation and lawful transfer: remove or pseudonymise personal data before it leaves, send only the fields monitoring needs, and put a valid transfer basis in place. A is a notice, not a safeguard. B protects the channel but still exports personal data. D removes a needed capability instead of making it compliant.

prompt: A hospital wants an assistant that answers clinicians' questions using patient records. Which consideration must be settled at the architecture stage rather than left for a later release?

options.text: The chunk size and overlap for the index built over the patient records
How protected health information flows end to end: storage, processing, access and audit under HIPAA
Which model tier to use for the first release of the assistant
The wording of the disclaimer shown to clinicians on first use

explanation: Correct: B. Regulated data flows are structural: where protected health information goes, which services touch it, access control and audit logging cannot be bolted on after launch without rebuilding the system. A, C and D can each be changed in a later release without rebuilding the system; the data-handling design cannot.

prompt: A tenant-screening assistant is found to rate applicants from certain neighbourhoods systematically lower, even though names and demographic fields were removed from its input. What does this most likely indicate, and what should be done?

options.text: The model is malfunctioning; restart the deployment and re-run all the affected applications through it again
The removed fields were not the problem; add them back so that the model has fuller context
A proxy such as postcode encodes a protected trait; audit inputs, measure outcomes by group, add fairness tests
The result is a statistical coincidence and no action is required until more data has been collected

explanation: Correct: C. Removing explicit demographic fields does not remove bias when other inputs act as proxies; the response is to find the proxies, measure outcomes by group and make fairness a standing part of evaluation. A treats a data problem as an outage. B reintroduces the direct features. D ignores a systematic disparity with legal and ethical consequences.

prompt: A security test of a document-assistant shows that text inside a retrieved PDF can change the assistant's behaviour: a planted instruction to reveal the system prompt partly succeeded. What is the correct architectural response?

options.text: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data: delimit it, say it holds no instructions, and enforce limits in code
Add a line to the system prompt saying the model must ignore any instructions found in documents, then close the issue
Scan incoming documents for the phrase "ignore previous instructions" and reject any document that contains it
Stop retrieving documents altogether and rely on the model's training knowledge to answer questions

explanation: Correct: A. Indirect prompt injection is a trust-boundary problem: content from outside is data, not instructions, and the real limits on what the system can do must be enforced in code regardless of what the model is persuaded to say. B relies on the prompt alone, which the test already showed is insufficient. C blocks one phrasing of an unbounded set. D removes the product's core capability.

prompt: An insurer deploys an AI assistant on its public website. Compliance asks how the design supports transparency obligations. Which measure addresses this most directly?

options.text: Making the assistant's replies sound as human as possible so that customers feel comfortable
Keeping the system prompt confidential so that competitors cannot copy the assistant's behaviour or tone
Using the largest available model so that the assistant's answers are more often correct
Disclosing that the customer is talking to an AI, stating its limits, and offering a route to a human

explanation: Correct: D. Transparency means users know they are dealing with an AI, understand what it can and cannot do, and can reach a person; this is what regulators and ethical guidelines ask for. A works against transparency. B is about confidentiality, not transparency. C is about accuracy, which is a different obligation.

prompt: A customer-service assistant must never include a customer's full card number in any reply, regardless of what the customer or a retrieved document says. Which control is the primary one?

options.text: A system-prompt instruction asking the model to be careful when handling card numbers
A human review of every reply before it is sent to the customer, regardless of content
A monthly audit of a random sample of sent replies to check whether any of them contain card numbers
A deterministic output filter outside the model that detects card-number patterns and redacts them

explanation: Correct: D. A hard "never" rule on a pattern that can be detected deterministically belongs in an output guardrail enforced in code; it works even when the model is manipulated. A is a soft control that can be overridden. C finds leaks a month later. B works but is disproportionate for a rule a regex can enforce.

prompt: A lending assistant produces loan-approval recommendations, each of which has significant financial and regulatory consequences. Which control should be primary?

options.text: An output filter that blocks any recommendation containing certain high-risk words or phrases
A dashboard showing the approval and rejection rates over time, reviewed by the risk team
A human decision-maker who reviews and owns each recommendation before it takes effect
A more detailed system prompt that describes the lending policy and its exceptions in full

explanation: Correct: C. For high-stakes, regulated decisions the primary control is human validation: the model recommends and a person decides. A catches surface patterns, not bad judgements. B is monitoring, which detects trends after decisions have been made. D improves inputs but leaves the model as the decision-maker.

prompt: Compliance must be able to show, months after the event, exactly what an agent did and why during a disputed transaction. Which control provides this?

options.text: A human approval step before each transaction the agent processes, recorded in the approval tool
An output filter applied to every reply the agent sends to the customer during the transaction
A rate limit on how many transactions the agent can process in any one hour, enforced by the gateway
An immutable, timestamped audit log of each step, tool call, input and decision, retained as required

explanation: Correct: D. Reconstructing a past decision needs a complete, tamper-evident record of the agent's steps kept for as long as regulation requires. A prevents some bad actions but does not record reasoning. B filters output rather than recording it. C limits volume and says nothing about any individual transaction.

prompt: A government agency wants to use a Claude-based assistant for internal case work and asks whether the deployment can meet FedRAMP requirements. What is the architect's correct first step?

options.text: Confirm the model and platform are offered in a FedRAMP-authorised environment and keep data inside it
Add a disclaimer to the assistant stating that it must not be used for sensitive or classified case data of any kind
Assume any cloud deployment is acceptable because the model provider is a large and well-known company
Run the model on employees' laptops so that the agency avoids cloud compliance obligations altogether

explanation: Correct: A. FedRAMP compliance is a property of the authorised environment: the architect must verify the platform's authorisation and keep the data within that boundary. B does not change where the data goes. C substitutes reputation for authorisation. D is neither possible for a hosted model nor a compliance strategy.

prompt: A product owner proposes that a Claude assistant give final answers on medication dosages to patients with no clinician involved, because "the model is very accurate". Which limitation of LLM systems most directly argues against this design?

options.text: LLMs cannot do the arithmetic that dosage calculations need reliably enough
LLM latency is too high for a patient-facing channel such as this one
LLMs can give confident, fluent answers that are wrong, so high-harm domains need human validation
LLMs cannot be used in healthcare at all under current regulation in any jurisdiction, so the design is illegal

explanation: Correct: C. The relevant failure mode is confident error: fluency is not accuracy, and where a wrong answer can cause serious harm the design needs human-in-the-loop validation. A and B are not the decisive limitation: latency is manageable and arithmetic can be checked in code; the problem is unvalidated confident error. D overstates the position; healthcare use is possible with appropriate controls.

prompt: A bank is deploying an assistant that drafts replies to customer complaints. Regulators require that no incorrect financial commitment reaches a customer. Which TWO controls most directly meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A system prompt asking the model to be careful and accurate about all financial matters
Human review and sign-off of every draft before it is sent
A larger model, which makes fewer factual mistakes when drafting replies
A deterministic check that flags amounts, dates and commitments so the reviewer must verify each against the account record
A faster response-time target so that customers receive replies to their complaints sooner

explanation: Correct: B and D. A "none may reach the customer" requirement calls for hard controls: a person accountable for each outgoing reply, and an automated check that catches commitments for verification. A and C reduce the error rate but cannot guarantee zero. E is unrelated to the requirement.

prompt: An architect is hardening a RAG agent with write tools against prompt injection carried in retrieved documents. Which TWO measures most reduce the risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Ask the model to rate how trustworthy each retrieved document seems before deciding whether to use it
Increase the number of retrieved chunks per query so that any injected text is diluted by the rest
Limit the agent's tools to the minimum needed and require confirmation for writes
Disable logging of retrieved content so that injected text is never stored in the trace system
Delimit retrieved content and tell the model it is data that may contain adversarial text

explanation: Correct: C and E. Defence in depth against injection combines reducing what a hijacked model can do (least privilege, confirmations on consequential actions) with making the trust boundary explicit in the prompt. A asks the model to police itself. B adds more untrusted text. D hampers investigation and prevents nothing.

prompt: A team is listing the risks of a new customer-facing assistant for a risk register. Which TWO are genuine LLM-system failure modes that belong on the register? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The model fabricates a policy clause that does not exist in the source documents
The model refuses to run without an internet connection on the user's own device
Answer wording varies between identical requests, which some users notice and remark on
A user's crafted input causes the assistant to ignore its scope and leak internal information
The model learns from each conversation and changes its own weights overnight

explanation: Correct: A and D. Hallucinated content and prompt injection are two of the central failure modes of LLM systems and each needs a mitigation on the register. B describes a hosted service in a confused way. C is ordinary sampling variance, not a failure mode. E is false: inference does not update the model's weights.

prompt: An HR software company runs an employee-support assistant built on Claude. Every prompt and response is written in full to a shared observability platform that most of the engineering organisation can query. Employees often mention health conditions, home addresses and salary details in their questions. The privacy team wants this fixed without losing the ability to debug and audit the assistant. Which change best addresses the concern?

options.text: Switch off prompt and response logging entirely, keeping only latency and error-rate metrics, so no personal data is ever written to the platform
options.explanation: This removes the data but also the traces needed to debug, evaluate and audit the assistant.

options.text: Redact or tokenise personal data in the logging pipeline before traces are stored, keeping any raw copy restricted with short retention
options.explanation: Redacting before persistence keeps traces useful for debugging while limiting who can see personal data and for how long.

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the assistant never to repeat names, addresses, health details or salaries back to employees in any of its replies
options.explanation: The employee's own message is still logged in full, and the instruction is a soft control on the output only.

options.text: Enable encryption at rest on the observability platform's storage volumes and rotate the encryption keys on a regular schedule managed by the security team
options.explanation: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks, not against the broad set of engineers who can query the logs.

explanation: Correct: B. The exposure comes from personal data being persisted in a widely accessible store, so the control belongs in the logging pipeline: redact or tokenise before storage, and keep any unredacted copy access-restricted with short retention. A throws away the observability the team needs. C only shapes the model's replies and leaves the employee's input logged. D addresses a different threat; authorised query users still see everything.

prompt: A European online-learning platform uses Claude to give feedback on student essays. Uploaded essays are chunked into a vector store for retrieval, conversations are kept in application logs, and frequent answers are held in a semantic response cache. A former student submits a GDPR erasure request. Which approach best supports honouring it?

options.text: Map each student identifier to every store that holds their data, including vector chunks, logs and cache entries, and then delete and verify in each
options.explanation: Erasure has to reach every derived copy, which is only practical if records are traceable to the person across stores.

options.text: Delete the student's account and essays from the primary database, since vector embeddings are numeric representations and are therefore not personal data
options.explanation: Embeddings and their stored chunk text can still relate to an identifiable person, so leaving them is a misconception.

options.text: Ask the model provider to remove the student's essays from the model, because the feedback the assistant gave was generated from that student's own writing
options.explanation: In this architecture the essays live in the platform's own stores, not in the model, so this targets the wrong place.

options.text: Leave the cache and logs to expire under their existing ninety-day retention settings, and delete only the vector store entries that are searchable
options.explanation: Waiting for routine expiry does not honour a specific request, and the logs still hold personal data meanwhile.

explanation: Correct: A. In a RAG system personal data is copied into derived stores (chunks and embeddings, conversation logs, caches), so erasure needs a data map that ties those copies back to the person, plus deletion and verification across each store. B wrongly treats embeddings and stored chunks as non-personal. C misplaces the data: it sits in the platform's stores, not the model. D relies on routine expiry instead of acting on the request.

prompt: An insurer uses Claude to triage around 20,000 low-value travel claims a day. Policy requires that a person makes every claim denial. Most claims are straightforward approvals, and the operations team cannot staff review of every decision. Which human-review design fits best?

options.text: Have reviewers examine a random five per cent of all decisions each day, and use the observed error rate to decide whether to tighten the prompt
options.explanation: Random sampling alone lets most denials go out without a person deciding them, breaching the policy.

options.text: Route every proposed denial, plus high-value or low-confidence cases, to mandatory review, and sample routine approvals to measure the error rate over time
options.explanation: Mandatory review where policy or risk demands it, plus sampling elsewhere, meets the rule and keeps workload manageable.

options.text: Require a reviewer to approve every single decision before it is sent, and hire temporary staff during peak travel seasons to keep the backlog under control
options.explanation: Full review would satisfy the rule but is disproportionate for routine low-value approvals the team cannot staff.

options.text: Ask the model to rate its own confidence for each claim, and finalise automatically any decision rated above 0.9, whether it is an approval or a denial
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and auto-finalising denials breaks the policy that a person decides them.

explanation: Correct: B. Human review should be risk-based: mandatory where policy or impact requires it (all denials, high value, uncertain cases) and sampled elsewhere to keep measuring quality. A lets denials through without a person. C meets the rule but at a cost the scenario rules out. D relies on uncalibrated self-ratings and lets the model finalise denials, which the policy forbids.

prompt: A public-sector benefits agency has caseworkers approve Claude-drafted eligibility decisions. Six months in, caseworkers accept 99.6% of drafts unchanged, with a median review time of nine seconds. An appeal reveals several approved drafts that misread income documents. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Treat the high acceptance rate as evidence that the drafts are accurate, and reduce review to a sample so caseworkers can handle more cases each day
options.explanation: High agreement with short review times signals rubber-stamping, not accuracy, and the appeal shows errors slip through.

options.text: Display the model's confidence score next to each draft so caseworkers can skim the confident ones and concentrate on the drafts the model is unsure about
options.explanation: Showing confidence tends to deepen anchoring on the model, and the misread drafts may well have looked confident.

options.text: Seed known-error cases to measure the review, show the source documents beside the key fields, and require reviewers to confirm each of those fields
options.explanation: This counters automation bias by making reviewers check evidence and by measuring whether review actually catches errors.

options.text: Add more caseworkers to the review team so that each one has a lighter daily workload and therefore more time available to spend on each draft decision
options.explanation: More time alone does not change the habit of accepting drafts, and nothing measures whether reviews improve.

explanation: Correct: C. Near-total acceptance in seconds, together with missed errors, is a classic sign of automation bias: the human gate exists on paper but not in practice. Seeding known errors measures whether review works, and presenting source evidence with required field confirmation makes the check real. A misreads rubber-stamping as accuracy. B strengthens anchoring on the model. D adds capacity without changing behaviour or measuring it.

prompt: An asset manager's research assistant answers analysts' questions about company filings. Analysts report that when they push back ("Are you sure? I thought margins rose"), the assistant often abandons a correct answer and agrees with them. What should the architect do?

options.text: Set temperature to zero so that the assistant gives the same answer each time the question is asked, which stops it from changing its mind under pressure
options.explanation: Lower temperature reduces sampling variation but does not address the model deferring to the user's pushback.

options.text: Ground answers in cited filing extracts, instruct the model to revise only on new evidence, and add pushback turns to the evaluation set
options.explanation: This targets sycophancy directly: evidence anchors the answer, and the eval measures whether it holds under pushback.

options.text: Move to the largest available model, on the basis that more capable models are confident enough in their reasoning not to agree with incorrect users
options.explanation: Capability may help, but assuming the problem is solved without grounding or measurement is not a control.

options.text: Disable follow-up messages so that each question is answered in a single turn, preventing analysts from challenging the answer in the same conversation
options.explanation: This removes a legitimate workflow, and analysts can still rephrase leading questions in a new turn.

explanation: Correct: B. Abandoning a correct answer under social pressure is sycophancy, a known LLM failure mode. Grounding claims in cited sources, telling the model to change its answer only when given new evidence, and testing pushback turns in evals address it and make it measurable. A confuses sycophancy with non-determinism. C assumes away the problem without evidence. D breaks the product and does not remove leading questions.

prompt: An accounting firm builds an assistant that answers staff questions about tax thresholds and filing deadlines. The rules change every year, and some changed after the model's training data was collected. Which design best addresses this limitation?

options.text: Add a line to the system prompt telling the model that it has up-to-date knowledge of all current tax rules and should answer with confidence
options.explanation: Telling the model it is current does not give it the new rules and makes confident wrong answers more likely.

options.text: Choose the most recently released model, since a newer model's training data will include the latest thresholds and deadlines for this tax year
options.explanation: Any model has a knowledge cutoff, and rules can change after it, so recency of release is not a control.

options.text: Retrieve the current rule text from a maintained source, cite it with its effective date, and say so when no current source is found
options.explanation: Retrieval supplies post-cutoff facts, and dated citations let staff verify which rules the answer relies on.

options.text: Ask staff to add the phrase "use the latest rules" to each question so the model knows it should prefer the current year's figures
options.explanation: The model cannot prefer rules it does not know, so the phrase changes nothing about its knowledge.

explanation: Correct: C. A model's knowledge stops at its training cutoff, so time-sensitive facts must be supplied at run time from a maintained source, with citations and effective dates, and with an explicit answer when nothing current is found. A and D only change wording and may increase confident errors. B ignores that every model has a cutoff and that rules keep changing after it.

prompt: A media company's consumer chatbot checks each user message with a moderation classifier before it reaches Claude. A red team shows that by escalating gradually over fifteen turns, each message individually harmless, they can steer the bot into producing content the policy forbids. Which change best closes this gap?

options.text: Extend the per-message classifier with a much longer list of blocked keywords and phrases taken from the red team's transcripts of the attack
options.explanation: The attack works because each message looks harmless on its own, so a bigger keyword list on single messages misses it.

options.text: Cap every conversation at three turns and start a fresh session after that, so that no attacker can build up context across a long exchange
options.explanation: This damages normal use and still allows attacks that fit in a few turns or are split across sessions.

options.text: Strengthen the system prompt with firm refusal instructions and remind the model to stay within the content policy no matter what users say
options.explanation: Prompt instructions help but are a soft layer, and the red team has already shown the model can be steered.

options.text: Screen the model's outputs and the whole conversation, not just individual messages, and add multi-turn attacks into the red-team test suite
options.explanation: Conversation-level and output-side checks catch harm that only emerges across turns, and regular tests catch regressions.

explanation: Correct: D. Multi-turn jailbreaks exploit checks that look at one message at a time, so guardrails need to evaluate the accumulated conversation and screen what the model actually produces, with multi-turn cases kept in the red-team suite. A still looks at single messages. B is a blunt restriction that hurts users and is easily worked around. C is a useful layer but not sufficient on its own.

prompt: A SaaS analytics product lets Claude write and run Python against CSV files that customers upload, so users can ask questions about their own data. Uploaded files may contain text crafted to manipulate the model. Where should the generated code run?

options.text: In the main application server, after asking Claude to review its own generated code for anything malicious before it is executed
options.explanation: Self-review by the same model that may have been manipulated is not an isolation boundary.

options.text: In the main application server process, with a blocklist that rejects any code importing modules such as os, socket or subprocess
options.explanation: Import blocklists are easy to bypass, and the code would still share the server's secrets and network.

options.text: In an isolated, short-lived sandbox per session, with no secrets, no other tenants' data, a restricted network and resource limits
options.explanation: Isolation contains whatever the code does, even if the model was manipulated into writing something harmful.

options.text: In one long-lived shared container per region, which keeps start-up fast, with every executed script logged for later security review
options.explanation: Sharing a container across tenants risks cross-tenant leakage, and logging only detects problems afterwards.

explanation: Correct: C. Model-generated code must be treated as untrusted, especially when inputs may carry injected instructions, so it should run in an isolated, ephemeral environment with no credentials, no cross-tenant access, limited egress and resource caps. A relies on the possibly manipulated model to police itself. B is a bypassable filter inside a privileged process. D shares state between tenants and only detects issues after the fact.

prompt: A retailer releases a new system prompt and model version for its shopping assistant to all users at once. Within an hour the assistant starts offering discount codes it is not authorised to give. Looking ahead, which capability would most limit the damage from a release like this?

options.text: A longer and more detailed system prompt that lists every situation in which the assistant must not offer a discount code to a customer
options.explanation: Better prompts may prevent this case but do nothing to contain the next unexpected regression.

options.text: Versioned prompt and model settings behind a flag, a staged rollout with monitoring, and a switch to revert or disable the discount tool
options.explanation: Staged rollout limits exposure, and a fast revert or tool kill switch stops harm without a full redeploy.

options.text: A weekly manual review of a sample of shopping conversations so the team can spot unusual behaviour and raise it at the next planning meeting
options.explanation: Weekly review finds the problem days later, long after the unauthorised discounts have been handed out.

options.text: A rule that any rollback must go through the full code-review and build pipeline, so that emergency changes are always reviewed before release
options.explanation: Requiring the full pipeline for a rollback slows containment exactly when speed matters most.

explanation: Correct: B. Prompt and model changes alter behaviour as much as code changes, so they should be versioned, rolled out gradually with monitoring, and be instantly revertible, with the ability to disable a risky tool on its own. A addresses one symptom only. C detects too late. D makes rollback slow when it needs to be immediate.

prompt: A recruitment platform uses Claude to score CVs against job requirements, and recruiters use the scores to build shortlists. Before launch, the client asks for evidence that the scoring does not disadvantage particular groups of candidates. Which testing approach provides that evidence?

options.text: Remove names and photos from every CV, then confirm that overall agreement between the model's scores and expert recruiters' scores is high
options.explanation: A high overall figure can hide large gaps between groups, and removing names does not remove proxies.

options.text: Tell the model in the system prompt to score fairly without regard to protected characteristics, then spot-check twenty scored CVs by hand
options.explanation: An instruction is not evidence, and twenty spot checks cannot reveal differences between groups.

options.text: Score matched CV pairs differing only in group-linked details, compare per-group score and error rates to thresholds, rerun on changes
options.explanation: Counterfactual pairs and per-group metrics show whether outcomes differ by group, and reruns catch regressions.

options.text: Rely on the model provider's published bias evaluations, since these cover the model's behaviour across a wide range of demographic groups
options.explanation: General model evaluations do not test this specific prompt, rubric and population, which is what the client needs.

explanation: Correct: C. Fairness evidence for a specific use case comes from testing that use case by subgroup: counterfactual pairs that vary only group-linked details, per-group score and error-rate comparisons against agreed thresholds, and repeat runs whenever the prompt or model changes. A reports an aggregate that can mask disparities. B offers an instruction and an anecdote. D is about the base model, not this application.

prompt: A small-business lender uses Claude to help underwriters assess loan applications. When an application is declined, the lender must give the applicant the specific main reasons, and those reasons must reflect what actually drove the decision. How should the system be designed to support this?

options.text: After a decline, send the application back to Claude with a request to explain why it was declined, and pass that explanation on to the applicant
options.explanation: A post-hoc explanation may be a plausible rationalisation rather than what actually drove the decision.

options.text: Enable extended thinking for each assessment and forward the model's reasoning text to declined applicants as the explanation for the decision
options.explanation: Raw reasoning text is not written as an applicant explanation and is not assured to reflect the true basis.

options.text: Send every declined applicant a standard letter saying that the decision was based on a range of factors assessed by the lender's underwriting team
options.explanation: A generic statement does not give the specific reasons the lender is required to provide.

options.text: Score defined policy criteria as structured fields with linked evidence, base the decision on them, and generate reasons from those recorded fields
options.explanation: Reasons drawn from the recorded criteria that drove the decision are specific, faithful and auditable.

explanation: Correct: D. For adverse decisions the explanation must match the actual basis, so the decision should be built from explicit, recorded criteria with linked evidence, and the reasons generated from those same fields for an underwriter to confirm. A invites a post-hoc rationalisation. B treats reasoning text as a faithful, applicant-ready explanation, which it is not designed to be. C fails the requirement for specific reasons.

prompt: A US health-technology company plans to send patient intake notes containing protected health information (PHI) to the Claude API to produce clinician summaries. Which TWO steps should be settled before any PHI is sent? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Confirm a business associate agreement (BAA) is in place with the provider and covers the specific services and features used
options.explanation: HIPAA requires a BAA with vendors handling PHI, and coverage can depend on which features are used.

options.text: Rely on TLS encryption between the application and the API, since encrypting data in transit is what HIPAA requires for sending PHI to a vendor
options.explanation: Encryption in transit is one safeguard, not a substitute for a BAA and the other HIPAA requirements.

options.text: Send only the fields the summary needs, and ensure the company's own logs, traces and caches holding PHI are under HIPAA-grade controls
options.explanation: Minimising PHI and securing the company's own copies covers the parts of the system it is responsible for.

options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt telling Claude not to retain or remember any patient information after the summary has been returned
options.explanation: Data retention is governed by the provider's terms and infrastructure, not by an instruction to the model.

options.text: Assume no agreement is needed, because the provider states that API inputs are not used for training by default, so PHI never leaves the request
options.explanation: Not training on inputs does not remove the need for a BAA when a vendor processes PHI.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Sending PHI to a vendor requires a BAA that covers the services actually used, and the company must minimise the PHI it sends and protect its own copies in logs, traces and caches. B treats one technical safeguard as the whole requirement. D confuses model behaviour with provider data handling. E mistakes a training policy for a contractual agreement covering PHI processing.

prompt: An education company is launching a Claude-based homework tutor for pupils aged 11 to 16. The safeguarding lead wants layered guardrails rather than reliance on the model alone. Which TWO controls are correctly placed? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Screen pupils' messages on the way in only, since if every input that reaches the model is acceptable then every reply the tutor produces will be acceptable too
options.explanation: Harmless inputs can still produce unsuitable outputs, so input screening alone leaves a gap.

options.text: Screen pupils' messages for signs of self-harm or abuse before the model replies, and route those to a human safeguarding workflow
options.explanation: An input-side check is the right place to catch disclosures that need a person, not just a model reply.

options.text: Check each generated reply for age-inappropriate content before it is shown, independently of whatever checks were applied to the pupil's input
options.explanation: An independent output check catches unsuitable replies however they arose, adding a second layer.

options.text: Put all of the safeguarding rules into the system prompt and drop the separate classifiers, which reduces latency and keeps the rules in one place
options.explanation: The system prompt is a soft layer, and removing independent checks leaves no defence if the model is steered.

options.text: Screen replies only after they have been displayed to the pupil, so the output check never adds latency to the tutoring conversation
options.explanation: A check that runs after display cannot stop unsuitable content from reaching the pupil.

explanation: Correct: B and C. Layered guardrails put independent checks on both sides of the model: input screening that routes safeguarding disclosures to people, and output screening that blocks unsuitable replies before display. A assumes clean inputs guarantee clean outputs. D collapses the layers into a single soft control. E runs the output check too late to prevent harm.

prompt: A logistics company deploys an agent to triage its accounts-payable inbox. Its tools can read email, send email, delete email, update supplier bank details and issue payments. Fraudsters regularly send emails impersonating suppliers and asking for bank details to be changed. Which TWO measures best reduce the risk from the agent's excessive agency? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Instruct the agent in its system prompt to be especially suspicious of emails asking for bank details to change, and to double-check them before acting
options.explanation: A prompt instruction can be defeated by a convincing or injected email, so it cannot be the main control.

options.text: Remove the payment and delete-email tools, since triage does not need them, and hand payments to a separate workflow with human approval
options.explanation: Removing capabilities the task does not need shrinks what a manipulated agent can do.

options.text: Add a confidence parameter to every tool so the agent must state how certain it is before each call, and reject calls below a set threshold
options.explanation: Self-declared confidence is easy for a manipulated agent to inflate and enforces nothing.

options.text: Have the backend hold any bank-detail change as pending until staff verify it with the supplier through a contact number already on file
options.explanation: An out-of-band check enforced outside the model stops fraudulent changes even if the agent is fooled.

options.text: Send every tool call to the security team's monitoring system for review at the weekly risk meeting, with alerts for unusual volumes
options.explanation: Monitoring helps detect abuse, but weekly review comes after the fraudulent payment has gone out.

explanation: Correct: B and D. Excessive agency is reduced by giving the agent only the tools its task needs and by enforcing high-risk actions outside the model, here with an out-of-band verification that the backend requires before a bank change takes effect. A and C rely on the agent's own judgement, which is what the fraud targets. E is detective and too slow to prevent the loss.

prompt: During discovery, a client's sponsor insists the assistant must be "100% accurate" before it can go live. What is the architect's most effective response?

options.text: Agree to the target and plan to keep testing until no further errors can be found in the test set
Explain that probabilistic systems have an error rate, then agree accuracy targets per use case and controls
Decline the engagement, since a requirement of perfect accuracy cannot be met by any system and the sponsor will not budge
Promise the target now and renegotiate once the system is built and the real numbers are known

explanation: Correct: B. Expectation alignment means being honest about the nature of the system and turning an impossible absolute into a measurable target plus controls for the residual risk. A sets up a failure at launch. C abandons a solvable conversation. D damages trust when the renegotiation comes.

prompt: A client opens an engagement with "we want an AI agent for our warehouse". Before proposing any architecture, what should the architect do first?

options.text: Draft a proposal for a multi-agent warehouse system based on common patterns seen across the industry
Build a quick prototype agent to show the client what is technically possible today
Run structured discovery: interview the people, map the process, find the problems and measures
Ask the client which model they would prefer to use so that the design can be sized around it

explanation: Correct: C. A vague request needs structured discovery before design: who is affected, what the process looks like today, what hurts, and how success will be measured. A and B commit to a solution before the problem is understood. D asks an implementation question at the wrong time.

prompt: A finance director instructs the team to use the cheapest model for a document-analysis solution that feeds regulatory filings. Testing shows the cheapest model has a materially higher error rate on this task. What should the architect do?

options.text: Present the error rates, cost difference and filing consequences, recommend the model that meets the bar
Comply with the instruction, since budget decisions belong to the finance director and not to the architect or the team
Quietly use the more capable model and absorb the extra cost in another budget line to avoid conflict
Escalate to the finance director's manager and ask for the instruction to be overruled on quality grounds

explanation: Correct: A. Communicating a trade-off means putting the evidence and consequences in front of the decision-maker and making a clear recommendation; the business then owns the choice. B hides a material risk. C is dishonest and will surface later. D jumps the stakeholder before the evidence has been presented to them.

prompt: A stakeholder demands complete answers in under one second from an assistant that performs multi-step retrieval and reasoning. Engineering analysis shows the pipeline cannot finish in under three seconds. Which approach best manages this?

options.text: Accept the one-second target and hope that the model provider's latency improves before launch
Remove the retrieval step so that the target can be met, and accept the lower accuracy that results from it
Ignore the demand, since it is technically unreasonable and will be forgotten once the system ships
Share the analysis, offer options such as streaming or a simpler fast mode, and agree an SLA

explanation: Correct: D. Managing an SLA expectation means showing the evidence, explaining the trade-off, and offering concrete alternatives that preserve what the stakeholder actually values, then agreeing a measurable target. A sets up a missed commitment. B trades away quality without discussion. C leaves the stakeholder uninformed and unaligned.

prompt: A consultancy is handing a completed assistant to the client's own engineers, who will run it from now on. Beyond the source code, which set of artefacts matters most for a successful handoff?

options.text: The sales proposal and the original statement of work that defined the engagement's scope
The chat transcripts the consultancy's team used with their AI tools while building the system over the engagement
A recording of the final demo and the slide deck that was presented to the steering committee
Architecture docs with decision records, runbooks, the evaluation suite, and a prompt-iteration guide

explanation: Correct: D. A team that will operate and evolve the system needs to know how it is built and why, how to run and recover it, how to tell whether a change made it better, and how to change prompts without regressing. A, B and C are historical artefacts that do not help anyone operate or improve the system.

prompt: Three months after launch, the sponsor's interest in an assistant is fading. The fortnightly report lists token spend, latency and uptime, and nothing else. What change would most improve alignment?

options.text: Report business outcomes the sponsor cares about, such as cases resolved and hours saved, with the technical metrics
Send the report every week instead of every fortnight so that the sponsor hears from the team more often and stays engaged
Add more technical metrics such as cache hit rate, p99 latency and error budgets to the existing report
Stop sending written reports and schedule a quarterly review meeting with the sponsor instead

explanation: Correct: A. Stakeholder feedback loops stay healthy when the reporting speaks to the outcomes the sponsor signed up for; technical metrics alone show cost without value. B and C send more of the same. D reduces contact instead of fixing its content.

prompt: Which lifecycle phase does this activity belong to: interviewing claims handlers to learn how claims are triaged today and where delays occur?

options.text: Design
Handoff
Monitoring
Discovery

explanation: Correct: D. Learning how the work is done today and where it hurts is discovery, which comes before any solution is designed. A would be choosing patterns and components. B is the transfer of a finished system to its operators. C is observing a system in production.

prompt: Which lifecycle phase does this activity belong to: reviewing a month of production evaluation results and choosing the next set of prompt changes to make?

options.text: Iteration
Discovery
Handoff
Design

explanation: Correct: A. Using production evidence to decide the next improvements is iteration, the phase that follows monitoring and keeps the system improving after launch. B is understanding the problem before building. C is transferring ownership. D is choosing the architecture before it is built.

prompt: An architect must explain to a non-technical steering committee why the team chose retrieval over fine-tuning for a policy assistant. Which way of communicating the decision is most effective?

options.text: Walk the committee through the embedding model benchmarks and the vector index configuration in detail, with slides
State the decision only, since the committee does not need to understand the technical reasoning
Frame it in the committee's terms, such as speed of policy updates, cost and auditability, and record the trade-offs
Send the committee the technical design document and invite any questions they may have by email

explanation: Correct: C.
